note:
The gospel of Luke, as shown by the reference to Theophilus (Luke 1:3).

**all that Jesus began to do and teach.** A fitting summary of what Luke records in his gospel. The verb “began” implies that this second book continues the account of Jesus’ deeds and teaching, now in new ways appropriate to His ascension to God’s right hand and the sending of God’s Spirit. Having completed His mission, it has been made clear that Jesus was more than “a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19). The ministry of the apostles in the early years of the church further confirms that fact.

Luke 24:50–52 locates the ascension near Bethany, on the east side of the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem.

**commands through the Holy Spirit.** After the resurrection, Jesus communicated to His apostles the reality of His resurrection (John 20; 21), the truth of His calling as Messiah (Luke 24:44–49), the blessing of the Holy Spirit (John 20:22, 23), and the reality of His physical resurrection body (Luke 24:37–43). The mention of the Holy Spirit during the forty days between Jesus’ resurrection and His ascension, before Pentecost, prepares readers for that promised event (v. 5; 2:1–11).

**he had chosen.** A reference to Jesus’ original choice of His apostles (Luke 6:12–16), one of whom (Judas) Jesus knew would become a traitor. This reminder sets the background for the church’s prayer later in this chapter, asking the ascended Jesus to reveal His choice of a replacement for Judas (Acts 1:24, 25).

Christ’s resurrection appearances (Matt. 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20; 21; 1 Cor. 15:5–7) were important as an unshakable confirmation of Christ’s supernatural person and work. It was important that Jesus’ resurrection be seen by the disciples, preparing them to be witnesses to His resurrection (v. 22; 2:32; 3:15; see Luke 1:2).

**forty days.** The time from the resurrection to the ascension. After Jesus ascended to heaven, the disciples stayed ten days in Jerusalem waiting for the promised outpouring of the Holy Spirit that occurred on Pentecost, the fiftieth day after Passover.

Jesus often communed with His friends and disciples over a meal: at the feeding of the five thousand (Luke 9:16), with tax collectors and sinners (Mark 2:15, 16; Luke 5:29), at the Pharisee’s house (Luke 7:37), at the Last Supper (Matt. 26:21, 26), and after the resurrection (Luke 24:42; John 21:9–15).

**wait for the promise of the Father.** The Holy Spirit is the gift of the Father as promised in the OT (Luke 24:49; cf. Is. 32:15; 44:3; Joel 2:28, 29) and the gift of Jesus the Son (John 14:15–17, 26; 15:26).

. John the Baptist baptized crowds of people (Matt. 3:5, 6, 13–15; Mark 1:5, 9; Luke 3:7–16, 21). John’s water baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4) pointed forward to the messianic baptism with the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). See theological note “The Baptism of Jesus” on p. 1733.

**not many days from now.** A few days will pass before Pentecost.

verse_quote: at this time restore the kingdom to Israel.
note: From what Jesus said in Matt. 19:28, the disciples thought that He might overthrow the Romans and restore the physical kingdom to Israel. As Jesus approached Jerusalem, they had expected that God’s reign would arrive in physical force (Luke 19:11), only to have their hopes dashed by Jesus’ death (24:21). Now that He has returned to life, their reborn hope still focuses narrowly on ethnic Israel.

verse_quote: not for you to know times or seasons.
note: The specific years or dates (which some in all ages try to predict) of the second coming of Christ (cf. 1 Thess. 5:2). Jesus made the same point before His death (Mark 13:32). Here Jesus shows how wrong their assumption is that they could pinpoint that the end-time completion of the kingdom is imminent. Rather, only the Father knows the timing of such things. Furthermore, the following context reveals an “already and not yet” eschatology, the idea that the last days have _already_ been inaugurated (Acts 2:17–21 note), but _not yet_ brought to their consummation or final end.

Jesus also described this event as His disciples’ being “clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). The Spirit’s power is exhibited not only in miracles but also in believers’ boldness to speak the gospel (Acts 3:12; 4:7, 33).

**Holy Spirit has come upon you.** The Holy Spirit will show His presence and power in their lives with visible and audible manifestations: the blowing of a violent wind, the appearance of tongues of fire, and speaking in foreign languages in an expansion of the prophetic gift to all God’s people, as predicted in Joel 2:28–32 (Acts 2).

**my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.** Jesus’ words forecast the geographical expansion of the church narrated in the book of Acts. The Jerusalem witness (ch. 2) gives in miniature form God’s worldwide ministry: “Jews ... from every nation” (2:5) and Gentile proselytes (v. 11) who hear and believe carry the message far and wide. In the rest of Acts, the gospel spreads throughout Jerusalem (3:1–8:1), then to Judea and Samaria, including Antioch of Syria (8:1–12:25), and finally to the ends of the earth (13:1–28:31). Recall that Acts 1:8 is an outline for the entire book (see the Introduction to Acts: Literary Features).

See theological note “The Ascension of Christ” on p. 1842. That a “cloud took Him” perhaps is an echo of Dan. 7:13 (the Son of Man coming on the clouds to receive a kingdom in heaven) and Jesus’ further fulfillment of it.

In the NT, people dressed in white or radiant clothing are commonly supernatural or glorified beings: Jesus Christ (Matt. 17:2; Mark 9:3; Rev. 1:14), angels (Matt. 28:3; Mark 16:5; Luke 24:4; John 20:12), and glorified saints (Luke 9:30, 31; Rev. 3:4, 5, 18; 4:4; 7:14). Here, as at the empty tomb, the “men” are angels, supernatural messengers sent from God’s heavenly court.

Eleven of Jesus’ disciples were from Galilee; Judas Iscariot was likely from Kerioth in Judah.

**in the same way.** Jesus will return in His resurrection body, coming with the clouds of heaven (Matt. 24:30; 26:64; Mark 14:62; 1 Thess. 4:16, 17; Rev. 1:7). See theological note “The Return of Christ” on p. 2137.

A hill beyond the Kidron Valley just east of the walled city of Jerusalem. The disciples had been with Jesus on the Mount of Olives near Bethany (Luke 24:50).

**a Sabbath day’s journey.** From the city, a distance calculated by the rabbis to be about 1,100 meters or three-fourths of a mile.

verse_quote: up to the upper room, where they were staying.
note:
Probably where the disciples have been hiding for fear of the Jews (John 20:19), although not continually (Luke 24:53). This may be the same room in which they celebrated the Passover and Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper (Mark 14:15), or a room in the house of Mary, the aunt of Barnabas and mother of John Mark (Col. 4:10), where the Christians later held meetings (Acts 12:12; 13:5). It was probably located close to the temple courts where the visiting Jewish crowds were assembled (2:5–12).

**Peter and John and James and Andrew.** The names of the Eleven are repeated (see Luke 6:14–16) to set the scene for the choice of a replacement for Judas the traitor (Acts 1:15–26).

**Bartholomew.** Also known as Nathanael (John 1:45; 21:2).

**James the son of Alphaeus.** Also known as James the younger (Mark 15:40).

**Zealot.** Possibly referring to Simon’s former membership in the Zealot revolutionary group.

**Judas the son of James.** Also known as Thaddaeus (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18), identified by his father’s name to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord.

Jesus established a pattern of prayer in the lives of His disciples. For examples of Jesus’ praying, see Luke 3:21; 5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28, 29; 11:1; 22:32, 41; 23:34, 46. In view of the promise of the Spirit’s imminent arrival (1:4, 5, 8) and Jesus’ assurance that the Father will give the Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11:13), we may infer that the outpouring of the Spirit by Jesus is likely the main subject of their petitions. Acts repeatedly records the church and its leaders at prayer (1:24, 25; 2:42; 4:23–31; 6:4, 6; 11:5; 12:5–17; 13:2, 3; 14:23; 16:25; 20:36; 21:5).

**with the women.** Certain women who have followed Jesus, supported His work, and cared for Him at His death (Matt. 27:55, 56; 28:1; Mark 15:40, 41; Luke 8:2, 3; 23:49; 23:55–24:1; 24:22). The group of believers, numbering about 120 (v. 15), includes both men and women, and God will soon pour out His prophetic Spirit on His male and female servants (2:18).

**Mary the mother of Jesus.** This is the last reference in the NT to Jesus’ mother.

**his brothers.** Jesus’ half-brothers, the sons of Mary and Joseph (Matt. 13:55; Luke 14:26; John 7:3, 10; see Gal. 1:19; Jude 1). As the text note indicates, the Greek equivalent of “brothers” is sometimes inclusive of male and female siblings, biological or spiritual; so it is possible that Jesus’ sisters are also included (Mark 6:3).
The ten days between the ascension and Pentecost (2:1).

Here, in contrast to vv. 14, 15, the Greek is literally “males, brothers.” Males are particularly addressed here because Peter is talking about replacing Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve whom Jesus originally chose as apostles (Matt. 10:2–4).

**the Scripture had to be fulfilled.** Pss. 69:25 and 109:8, quoted in v. 20, are applied by Peter to Judas Iscariot, who as an enemy of God was deposed from his apostleship. Now “his office” (Ps. 109:8) must be filled again. The fulfillment of Scripture is necessary because God reveals His inviolable purpose in His word, as Jesus taught His apostles (Luke 22:37; 24:25–27, 44–49).

**the Holy Spirit spoke ... by the mouth of David.** The Holy Spirit inspired David to compose these words using his poetic skills, a concise expression of the complete collaboration of Scripture’s divine and human authors (see 4:25).

Luke 22:3 mentioned that Judas as “of the number of the twelve,” a number that was symbolically significant for its association with Israel’s twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). That apostolic number must be restored to completion before the Spirit comes, since Is. 32:15 prophesied that the Spirit would restore Israel, and the twelve apostles represent Israel in miniature. This shows that the restoration of Israel is beginning with the pouring out of the Spirit and includes Gentiles (cf. Acts 10:44–47; 11:15, 16, which show that the Gentiles are part of the Joel 2:28–32 prophecy about Israel’s restoration).

**allotted his share in this ministry.** In His plan, God allowed Judas, the enemy of the Savior, to serve for a time in the ministry of the disciples (Luke 9:1–6).

Judas indirectly bought the field when he returned the money to the chief priests and elders, who in turn purchased a burial place for foreigners called the “Field of Blood.” See Matt. 27:5–8.

**with the reward.** The thirty silver coins (Matt. 26:15), probably worth about 120 denarii, or 120 days’ labor (Matt. 20:2). The amount represents how cheaply Israel’s leaders value the Lord and His messengers (Zech. 11:12–14).

**falling headlong.** Matthew writes that Judas “hanged himself” (Matt. 27:5). Apparently some time after the hanging his bloated body fell to the ground and ruptured, vividly signifying Judas’s self-made condemnation.

Ps. 69:26 is fulfilled in that Judas’s final property purchase was a graveyard, where the dead, not the living, dwell.

**his office.** InPs. 109, King David invokes God’s judgment on those who repaid his goodness with evil and his love with hatred (v. 5), as Judas did to Jesus the Messiah. Among the curses on such a traitor was the reassignment of his office, or “position of oversight,” to another (v. 8), as the church now asks the ascended Jesus to do in choosing Judas’s successor.

This includes the whole time of Jesus’ public ministry from His baptism to His ascension. Such extensive and intimate association with the band of Jesus’ closest followers will qualify this new apostle to bear credible eyewitness testimony that the same Jesus who taught and healed over three years before His crucifixion has indeed been raised from the dead (v. 22).
Evidently Joseph and Matthias are chosen from a larger number of witnesses as meeting the criteria laid out by Peter in vv. 21, 22. Neither is mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.

The mention of Jesus’ choice of His apostles in v. 2 shows that, within weeks of His resurrection and days of His ascension, the church was addressing Him in prayer as “Lord,” and confessing His divine knowledge of the secrets of all human hearts (1 Sam. 16:7; Prov. 24:12; Luke 6:8; 9:47; 11:17; 16:15; Heb. 4:13). This demonstrates, contrary to the assertions of some, that belief in Jesus’ deity goes right back to the primitive church and was not a later invention.

**you have chosen.** Although Christ’s choice of other categories of church leaders will be mediated through the discernment of other believers (6:3–6; 14:23), in the case of apostles the choice must be indicated by Jesus Himself through direct revelation (1:2; Luke 6:12–14; Gal. 1:1, 11–16). Therefore, having prayed, the believers resort to an ancient form of seeking disclosure of God’s secret purpose (v. 26 note).

Lots are mentioned in the OT as a means of ascertaining God’s will (Josh. 7:16–18; 1 Sam. 10:20–21). Presumably the Urim and Thummim kept by the high priest had this function (Ex. 28:30 note; Num. 27:21; 1 Sam. 14:41).

**apostles.** See theological note “The Apostles” on previous page.

Lit. the “fiftieth day” after the Sabbath of the Passover week (Lev. 23:4–7, 15, 16). Pentecost was celebrated on the first day of the week and was one of the three great annual feasts of Israel, preceded by Passover (Lev. 23:4–8; Num. 28:16–25) and followed four months later by the Feast of Booths (Lev. 23:33–43; Num. 29:12–38; cf. John 7:1–44). Pentecost is also called the Feast of Weeks, because it was celebrated seven weeks after Passover (Deut. 16:10); the Feast of Harvest, because the first fruits of the harvest were gathered then (Ex. 23:16); and the “day of the firstfruits” (Num. 28:26). In Jewish tradition this feast was associated with the giving of the law, since Israel reached Mount Sinai about two lunar months after crossing the Red Sea (Ex. 19:1).

**they were all together.** All of the apostles (1:16) were there, as were the women, Jesus’ relatives (1:14), and the 120 mentioned earlier (1:15).

verse_quote: a sound like a mighty rushing wind.
note: Three signs (wind, fire, and inspired speech) of God’s presence were witnessed (Ex. 3:2; 13:21; 24:17; 40:38; 1 Kin. 19:11–13). Wind is a symbol of the Holy Spirit’s presence (Ezek. 37:9, 13; John 3:8), while fire is a symbol of His cleansing and judging power (Matt. 3:11, 12). The tongues were various languages spoken in all parts of the eastern Mediterranean region, from Rome to Persia. Jewish tradition associated wind, fire, and even the announcement of the law in various tongues with Mount Sinai (Ex. 19:16–20; Deut. 4:33).

All of the 120 (1:15). Joel 2:28, cited in v. 17, speaks of God’s Spirit poured out “on all flesh,” sons and daughters, young and old.

**filled with the Holy Spirit.** They were under the special guidance and influence of the Spirit, particularly evidenced in the gift of prophecy (vv. 11, 17, 18) delivered in human languages (“tongues,” v.4; “native language,” v. 8) that they had not previously learned (see 10:46; 19:6). Paul discusses the spiritual gift of tongues in 1 Cor. 12–14. The coming of the Spirit is the fulfillment of Jesus’ promise reported in 1:5, 8 and Luke 24:49, but this does not mean that the Holy Spirit was not present and working with God’s people in the OT (“Holy Spirit” occurs in Ps. 51:11; Is. 63:10, 11; “Spirit of the Lord” in Judg. 3:10; 1 Sam. 10:6; Is. 11:2).

**the Spirit gave them utterance.** In all of the Christian life, nothing is accomplished apart from God (Eph. 2:10; Phil. 2:12, 13).

The fact that all of the Jews present hear the apostles speak in their own language points to Pentecost being a reversal of God’s judgment at Babel (Gen. 11:1–9). In order to prevent human beings from uniting together as a collective whole in opposition to God and His people, the Lord confused the languages of humanity at Babel, separating the human race into various groups, each with its own language. In Christ, human beings from every tribe and tongue are reunited as one people of God in service to His kingdom.

**2:5 Jews, devout men.** See 8:2; 22:12; Luke 2:25. Probably some of these are visiting Jerusalem for the feast: but the crowd apparently includes many from the dispersion who had taken up residence in Jerusalem, since Peter accuses his audience of complicity in the killing of Jesus (vv. 14, 22–23).
The crowd is amazed that rural Galileans, with their peculiar accents and presumably inferior education, could have learned all these foreign languages., 7

The list of people from fifteen nations starts with the east (“Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia,” where Jews had been taken captive to Assyria and Babylon). The list proceeds west to Judea, and then north to Asia Minor (“Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia”), from there to North Africa (“Egypt and parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene”), then to Rome. Finally the list includes two widely separated places, Crete (an island in the Mediterranean Sea) and Arabia (a desert region on the fringe of the empire).

Longtime residents of Jerusalem, not recognizing the patterns of foreign languages, cynically conclude that the believers’ speech has resulted from drunkenness. The same work of God that has enabled speakers of “Gentile” languages to hear God’s word conceals it from others (1 Cor. 14:21–23).
Counting 6 a.m. as the first hour makes this 9 a.m. In the apostles’ era it is customary to fast on feast days until at least the fourth hour, making the alleged drunkenness most unlikely.

The quotation is from the Septuagint’s translation of Joel 2:28–32 (3:1–5 LXX). Peter’s use of the words “in the last days” (cf. Is. 2:2; Hos. 3:5; Mic. 4:1; 1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Tim. 3:1; 1 Pet. 1:20; 1 John 2:18) makes explicit that Joel is referring to the last times promised by God. Peter interprets Joel’s words as referring to the new covenant in contrast to the former days of the old covenant (Heb. 8:7; 9:1). Through Joel, God promised to extend the gift of prophecy to all His people, young and old, male and female. Thus the gift of tongues is understood to be a specific form of prophecy, the speaking of God’s mysteries in special revelation (1 Cor. 14:2–6).

This title is used elsewhere by Luke (6:14; 10:38; 22:8; 26:9; Luke 18:37; 24:19). In his sermon, Peter emphasizes these important facts about Jesus: His miraculous signs (v. 22), His repudiation by His own people and death at the hand of lawless Gentiles (v. 23), His bodily resurrection (vv. 24–32), His exaltation and enthronement at God’s right hand in heaven (vv. 33–36), His outpouring of the Spirit that very day (v. 33), and the final and total defeat of His enemies at His second coming (v. 35).

**attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs.** Although the fact that Jesus came from Nazareth has been a stumbling block to many (cf. John 1:46), God has amply demonstrated that He is the Messiah through the attestation of miracles.

verse_quote: according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.
note:
Although wicked men, both Jews and Gentiles (4:27, 28), put Jesus to death of their own will, their actions were within the sovereign determination of God (cf. 17:26; 2 Chr. 25:16; Jer. 21:10; Dan. 11:36). God ordained the death of His Son, but the immediate perpetrators bear the guilt for crucifying Jesus (3:17, 18; 4:27, 28; 13:27; see Luke 22:22). God ordains the means as well as the ends of human events without violating human freedom or removing human responsibility (Gen. 50:20). The Jews could not pass their guilt to the Romans; they asked the Romans to crucify Jesus. Peter teaches that unbelieving Jews are accountable (3:15; 4:10; 5:30; 10:39), as are Rome’s Gentile forces (4:25–28).

**crucified.** Luke again emphasizes how Jesus died (Luke 24:39). Archaeologists have discovered in Palestine the pierced heel bones of a first-century A.D. victim of crucifixion.

In Ps. 16, David is primarily speaking about his own human experience and suffering, but in the verses quoted here he is ultimately talking about Jesus (v. 25), God’s Holy One whose body did not see decay (v. 27) as David’s did (v. 29).
David’s prophetic gift enabled him to predict aspects of his descendant’s, the Messiah’s, experience, as the Holy Spirit spoke through his mouth (1:16; 4:25).

verse_quote: exalted at the right hand of God.
note:
God’s plan goes beyond the resurrection of His Son, who must be exalted to a position of sovereign authority at the right hand of God (cf. Ps. 110:1). The Son is now glorified with the glory He had before the world existed (John 17:5).

**and having received from the Father ... Holy Spirit ... poured out.** The doctrine of the Trinity is implied: Peter shows how the Father (vv. 32, 33) worked in the life, death, resurrection, and exaltation of Jesus, His Son, and the Holy Spirit produced the miracle of causing His servants to speak in tongues. Thus, Pentecost constitutes the fulfillment of John the Baptist’s announcement that Jesus would baptize people with the Holy Spirit (1:5; Luke 3:16).

As Jesus reminded the Jewish leaders, in Ps. 110:1 David spoke of the Messiah as his “Lord,” and therefore David’s superior, who would be seated at God’s right hand (Luke 20:41–44). Jesus’ ascension fulfilled this psalm and showed Him to be not merely David’s son but also David’s Lord—and Lord of all.

In this climactic statement, Peter declares not only that Jesus is God’s Messiah (3:18, 20; 4:26; 5:42; Is. 11:1; Luke 4:18–21), but also that He is the exalted Lord (Rom. 10:9; Phil. 2:9–11), and the conquering King (1 Cor. 15:24, 25; Rev. 19:16).

Repentance (turning to God in sorrow for sin) and baptism were important parts of the message of John the Baptist (Matt. 3:1; Mark 1:4) and of Jesus (Matt. 4:17; 11:20; Luke 13:3, 5), and they remain central in the church’s preaching and teaching (Matt. 28:18, 19). See theological note “Baptism” on p. 1988.

**in the name of Jesus Christ.** A summary of Matt. 28:18, 19 (baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), with only Jesus mentioned here, since Peter’s sermon has to do with Jesus and His ministry, and Peter’s hearers have particularly sinned against Jesus (vv. 23, 36). The use of the divine name distinguishes Christian baptism from the preparatory baptismal rite practiced by John.

**for the forgiveness of your sins.** Baptism is a sign and seal of the forgiveness of sins (Titus 3:5). The physical rite itself does not confer the spiritual blessing of forgiveness, but the readiness of Peter’s audience to submit to baptism expresses their faith in the Savior whom Peter has proclaimed. Peter’s extension of the promise to the children of believers (v. 29) is strong evidence that the new covenant sign of initiation—baptism—is to be applied to the children of believers under the new covenant, just as the old covenant sign of initiation—circumcision—was applied to the children of believers under the old covenant (Gen. 17:1–14; cf. Col. 2:11, 12).

**the gift of the Holy Spirit.** The gift of the indwelling person of the Holy Spirit, as well as the gift of forgiveness (Eph. 1:7), and of empowering for ministry. It is significant that Peter does not speak here of receiving the gift of tongues. The gift of the indwelling Holy Spirit is essential for producing the fruit of the Spirit in the lives of believers (Gal. 5:22, 23) and for exercising the gifts of ministry that the Spirit chooses to distribute to different believers (1 Cor. 12:4–11).

Peter proclaims that salvation through God’s Messiah is promised to the Jews, to their children, and to all those far off (i.e., the Gentiles; Eph. 2:11–13). Here again is the message of Acts—the gospel is for Jews and Gentiles. As in His covenant with Abraham, so now in the new covenant God’s promise includes the children of believers, although each individual and generation must personally embrace that promise by faith. The inclusion of children in the promise is part of the rationale for the practice of infant baptism, but baptism conveys no salvific benefits to baptized individuals who never come to saving faith (Eph. 2:8, 9). This is as true for those who are baptized after making a profession of faith in Christ as it is for those who are baptized before they profess faith. See theological note “Infant Baptism” on p. 41.

**everyone whom the Lord our God calls.** These words are drawn from Joel’s prophecy, immediately after the passage that Peter quoted previously. People must “call on the name of the Lord” for salvation (Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21), but ultimately God’s choice and calling enables them to call on Him (Acts 13:48; John 6:37; Eph. 1:4, 5).

Like the rest of the Bible, Acts teaches that God alone saves and that He does so only through Jesus Christ (vv. 21, 39; 4:11, 12). Nevertheless, as God opens hearts, human beings must and will respond to the gospel in repentance and faith (v. 38; 16:14, 15, 30–34). We must believe, but we will believe only if the Holy Spirit opens our hearts to rest in Christ alone (John 3:5–8).

**this crooked generation.** From the time of Moses (Deut. 32:5), this expression has characterized those who resist God’s Word in unbelief and defiant rebellion (Phil. 2:15).

verse_quote: the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
note: This is the first of a number of summaries, inserted between accounts of decisive events and characterizing the ongoing life of the early church (see 4:32–35; 6:7; 12:24; 13:49; 19:20). This initial survey of the activities to which believers single–mindedly devoted themselves summarizes the characteristics of the church’s life together and the essential elements needed in Christian discipleship. They are elements the apostles learned from their experience with Jesus: His teaching about His person and work (Matt. 16:18, 19; Luke 24:46) and their Christian responsibility as His followers (Matt. 5–7), the fellowship of Christ with His disciples (John 13), the Lord’s Supper (the breaking of bread; Matt. 26:17–30), and His prayer life for and with the disciples (Matt. 6:5–13; Luke 11:1–13; John 17). “Fellowship” here has a particular reference to the practice of sharing material resources with the needy, since the Greek word _koinōnia_ is echoed in v. 44: “they had all things in _common._” The “breaking of bread” could refer to shared meals generally (v. 46), but in this context refers to the Lord’s Supper (20:7; Luke 22:19; 24:30, 35).

This demonstrates the unity of the Spirit Paul later advocates (Eph. 4:3).

**all things in common.** On the connection with “fellowship,” see v. 42 note. As v. 45 and a later summary (4:32–35) with its context (4:36–5:11) clarify, the early church did not practice a mandatory communalism of property (such as that required of full members of the Qumran sect). Those who had property were free to retain it (see 2:46, where believers retain their houses) or to liquidate them to meet others’ needs (5:4; see 1 Tim. 6:17–19). The divine grace that they had received so unified their hearts that they gladly and freely shared with each other as needs arose.
Unified in the Spirit, the believers were sensitive to the physical needs of others and voluntarily (4:34; 5:4) gave to meet those needs.
In contrast to “the breaking of bread” in v. 42, this refers to the common daily meals shared in the homes of believers.
The church belongs to the Lord, and He is the one who sovereignly builds His church (Matt. 16:18; 1 Cor. 3:9; see Acts 5:14; 6:7; 11:21; 18:9, 10).

The temple courts, and particularly the part near the gate called Beautiful (v. 2). This may have been the Nicanor Gate made of Corinthian bronze. Its exact location is uncertain.

**the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.** That is, from dawn, so about 3 p.m., the time of the evening sacrifice, according to Jewish sources. The Roman centurion Cornelius in Caesarea apparently synchronized his prayer schedule with that of the temple (10:3, 30).
Like a lame man later healed through Paul at Lystra (14:8–18). The man’s congenital inability to stand or walk made the miracle more remarkable and undeniable (3:9, 10; 4:14; 22).
As Jews, Peter and John could walk through the Court of Women into the Court of Israel, but non-Jews would be restricted to the Court of the Gentiles.

verse_quote: the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.
note: This incident and its aftermath, the apostles’ arrest and hearing before the Sanhedrin, are permeated by references to the power of Jesus’ name (v. 16; 4:7, 10, 12, 17, 18, 30).

verse_quote: walking and leaping and praising God.
note: Jesus cited Is. 35:5, 6 and 61:1 to show the disciples of John the Baptist that His healing signs—including causing the lame to walk—demonstrated that He was indeed the promised Redeemer. The leaping of this formerly lame man fulfills Is. 35:6, part of a restoration prophecy about Israel, which harmonizes well with the restoration prophecies cited in Acts 1:8 and the citing of Joel 2:28–32 in Acts 2.

A porch built by Herod the Great along the east wall of the temple enclosure, in the Court of the Gentiles and thus outside the Court of Women and the Court of Israel. Jesus taught here on occasion (John 10:22, 23).

Rabbinic tradition spoke of individuals of such exceptional piety that God was obligated to grant their prayers, but Peter and John hastened to deflect attention from themselves and to insist that Jesus, the suffering and vindicated Servant of the Lord, was the agent of this healing, because of His resurrection power.

verse_quote: The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.
note:
Appeal to the patriarchs is important in the sermons of Christ’s servants, since Jesus’ redemptive mission is the fulfillment of God’s covenant promises to those fathers (7:32; 13:17).

**glorified his servant Jesus.** The term appears throughout the Septuagint of Isaiah 40–53 (about Israel’s future restoration to God) to designate the Lord’s servant, and in Is. 52:13, God says that His servant will be “exalted” (Gk. “glorified”). Jesus, as the true Servant who fulfills these servant passages, is glorified because of the restoration work that He performed. It is likely that Peter has Is. 49:3 specifically in mind, which prophesies that the Messiah would be God’s “servant, Israel in whom I will show My glory.” Isaiah said this “glory” would be shown in the Servant’s work of restoring Israel and the nations (Is. 49:4–6).

verse_quote: denied the Holy and Righteous One.
note: The phrase “the Holy One,” referring to God, appears a number of times in the OT. The phrase “the Holy One of Israel” occurs in Is. 1:4 and 5:24 (cf. Luke 1:35). Isaiah also speaks of God as “the Righteous One” (Is. 24:16; cf. Acts 7:52; 22:14). In applying this description to Jesus, Peter may be indicating the deity of Christ. In Is. 53:11 “the righteous one” also refers to God’s “servant,” whose undeserved suffering renders others righteous.

The Greek term can also be translated “leader” (5:31), “founder” (Heb. 2:10; 12:2), or “head” of a tribe (Ex. 6:14; Num. 10:4; etc.). It designates Jesus as the personal source of life and highlights the tragic irony that others killed Him.
. As the later failure and humiliation of Sceva’s sons will show, Jesus’ name is not a magic formula that “works” apart from faith in Him (19:13–16).

Their ignorance does not excuse their sin but it leaves open the possibility of repentance and forgiveness (1 Tim. 1:13, 14), whereas fully cognizant defiance seems to be irreversible (Mark 3:22–30; Heb. 6:4–6).

verse_quote: foretold by the mouth of all the prophets.
note: See Luke 24:26, 27, 44–47. Peter may have cited such passages as Deut. 18:15 (quoted in v. 22); Pss. 2; 16:8–11; 22 (cf. 1 Pet. 1:10, 11); and Is. 52; 53 (alluded to in vv. 13, 14).

Peter’s sermon illustrates the two sides of repentance, that is, turning aside in sorrow from sin, and turning to God in faith. The call to repentance and faith is a necessary element of apostolic preaching (2:38; 17:30; 20:21).

**sins ... blotted out.** In the order of the gospel, repentance and faith receive from God forgiveness and removal of sins (2:38).

This phrase, like “restoring all the things” (v. 21), could refer to the second coming of the Messiah. More likely the “refreshing” is synonymous with the coming and reception of the Holy Spirit that was prophesied by Isaiah (Is. 32:15; 44:3; 59:21), at which time the Spirit had been poured forth (notice the correlation of “forgiveness of sins” followed by “you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” in 2:38 and “that your sins may be wiped away” followed by “times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord” in 3:20). The “last days” began at Pentecost (2:17) and will be consummated at the time of “the restoring of all things” (v. 21) in the new heaven and earth (2 Pet. 3:8–13).

verse_quote: saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring.’
note: As a climax, Peter refers to another patriarch and prophet, Abraham, through whom God sent Abraham’s “offspring,” the Messiah (Gal. 3:16), to bless all peoples on earth.

Peter’s Jewish listeners are the first to receive blessing through Abraham’s offspring, God’s servant Jesus, and from them the blessing promised in the Abrahamic covenant will embrace “all the families of the earth” (13:46, 47; Rom. 1:16). As members of Abraham’s spiritual posterity, all those who belong to Christ are also called “Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. 3:29), which is another name for “Israel” (Gen. 21:12).

**turning every one of you from your wickedness.** Although human beings are responsible to turn from unbelief in repentance (v. 19), only God’s sovereign intervention can give repentance (5:31; 11:18), enabling people to make that turn toward Him.

Several priests serving their allotted week’s temple service (Luke 1:8, 23) are near Solomon’s Colonnade and can hear Peter’s declarations about Jesus the Messiah, which now specifically mentions the involvement of Jewish rulers, who had charge of the temple, in pressuring Pilate to execute Jesus (3:13, 14, 17). Alarmed at this critique of Judaism’s leaders, the priests probably alert the captain of the temple guard. This captain is the commander of the temple police force and a member of one of the important priestly families. The priests also alert the Sadducees, who hold prominent positions in the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council.

verse_quote: proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
note: The Sadducees are annoyed because the apostles are teaching the people about the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:12–20). Unlike the other first-century Jewish sects such as the Pharisees, the Sadducees did not believe in the bodily resurrection even at the end of history (23:6–8; Luke 20:27–40).

verse_quote: put them in custody ... for it was already evening.
note: This action is necessary because the temple sacrifices have concluded and the temple gates are closed; official actions by the Sanhedrin will have to be taken the next day.

Despite the persecution, the church has grown from three thousand on the day of Pentecost (2:41) to five thousand at the time Peter and John are arrested. The emphasis here is on men, probably as representative heads of households (Luke 9:14).

These groups constitute the Jewish religious council, the Sanhedrin. Luke 22:66 describes the body of chief priests and scribes as “their council.” This body includes the high priest and members of his family (v. 6); other Sadducees; Pharisees (Matt. 27:62) such as Nicodemus (a “ruler of the Jews” and “teacher of Israel,” John 3:1, 10) and Gamaliel (5:34; 22:3); and “elders” who, though neither priests nor scholars, are respected heads of Jerusalem’s aristocratic families.

The men listed in this verse constitute what might be called the executive committee of the council. Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas the official high priest (John 18:13), is here called the high priest. However, since the Romans deposed Annas in A.D. 15, he is not officially the high priest at this time; rather, he is the power behind the office and probably still regarded as rightful high priest by many Jews, for the high priest is supposed to serve for life. John is possibly Jonathan son of Annas, who was appointed high priest in A.D. 36, or Jonathan ben Zaccai, who became president of the Great Synagogue after the fall of Jerusalem. Nothing is known of Alexander.

The answer is given in v. 10: “the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.” The power of the name of Jesus (which reveals His person) is the central and unifying theme in the healing of the lame man and its aftermath. Jesus’ name or the name of the Lord is emphasized often throughout Acts (2:21, 38; 3:16; 4:10, 12, 17, 18, 30; 5:28, 40, 41; 8:16; 9:15, 28; 15:26; 16:18).

In Luke and Acts, this expression seems to refer to an intervention whereby the Spirit enables believers to speak God’s message (2:4; 4:31; 9:17; 13:9–11a; Luke 1:15, 41, 67). The holy character that the Spirit’s ongoing presence sustains in individuals distinguishes them as “full of the Holy Spirit” (6:3, 5; 7:55; 11:24; Luke 4:1; see Eph. 5:18).
In Acts, defense of the gospel often includes reference to the fulfillment of OT prophecy; here Ps. 118:22 is quoted (also cited in Matt. 21:42; 1 Pet. 2:7; cf. Rom. 9:33).

Just as the name of Jesus was the only hope for physical healing of the man crippled from birth, so also the name of Jesus is the only hope for the spiritual healing of mankind. This exclusive and total reliance upon Christ for salvation is the clear teaching of both Jesus and the apostles (John 14:6; 1 Tim. 2:5). See theological note “Salvation” on p. 2058.

The courage and ready witness of Peter and John is a fulfillment of Christ’s promise to the disciples in Matt. 10:19, 20. The courage and knowledge of the unschooled Galilean fishermen astonishes the Sanhedrin. In taking note that these men “had been with Jesus,” the council no doubt remembers how Jesus, though without formal training, likewise had surprised them with His teaching (Luke 2:46, 47; John 7:15).

verse_quote: to listen to you rather than to God.
note: Although God calls Christians to submit to authority structures that He has ordained for the family, the state, and the church (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–18), our obligation to God Himself has priority over the rights of the state or any human authority (Luke 14:26). The apostles affirm this principle even more strongly in Acts 5:29. See theological note “Civil Government” on p. 2004.

verse_quote: lifted their voices together to God.
note:
The whole church responds to the Sanhedrin’s threats with prayer, the natural result of the apostles’ training with Jesus and the habits they have formed (2:42).

**Sovereign Lord.** A term used to express the total creative power and control of the Lord over all His physical creation and over the affairs of humanity (cf. vv. 25, 26; Jer. 10:12).

**made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.** An echo of the description of the Lord in Ps. 146:5, 6, contrasting Him to princes, who cannot be trusted to save because their plans, like the princes themselves, are short-lived (vv. 3, 4).

verse_quote: through the mouth of our father David.
note: A succinct summary of verbal inspiration (see 1:16; Heb. 10:15). Scripture’s authors wrote under the guidance and control of the Spirit (2 Pet. 1:21).

verse_quote: your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed.
note:
At Jesus’ baptism the Father’s voice bound together His royal sonship as the Christ (anointed) (Ps. 2:7) with His identity as the well-pleasing and Suffering Servant (Is. 42:1; cf. Luke 3:22). So the church now recognizes Jesus as both anointed King and holy Servant.

**Herod and Pontius Pilate ... Gentiles ... peoples of Israel.** The believers properly understand that both Jews and Gentiles, with their rulers, are responsible for the crucifixion of Jesus, and recognize that Psalm 2 foreshadowed this multiethnic conspiracy against the Lord’s Anointed One, Jesus. The rulers were Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great and tetrarch (i.e., subordinate ruler under Rome) of Galilee and Perea (Luke 3:1; 23:6, 7), and Pontius Pilate, who was the Roman prefect (governor) of Palestine from A.D. 26 to 36 (Luke 3:1; 23:1–24).

Nothing, not even the wrongful death of God’s Son, happens apart from God’s sovereign will and control (see 2:23). The certainty of God’s plan for the world is established by His sovereign “plan” and ensured by His almighty “hand.” The early chapters of Acts teach the compatibility of divine sovereignty and human responsibility. While the murderers of Jesus acted in accord with what God had determined, they were morally responsible agents and accountable for their wickedness (3:15). Cf. Gen. 50:20.

This prayer illustrates the way in which the church should be emboldened and encouraged by God’s sovereignty. In the face of the threat of violence, the church affirms God’s control of the situation (v. 28) and, instead of requesting physical safety, they petition for greater boldness to testify to God’s gospel.

**Lord.** The word for “Lord” is _kyrios,_ used in the Septuagint to translate the divine name _Yahweh._ It is used in the NT to refer both to God and also to Christ specifically (2:36; 7:31).
See 2:4 and 4:8 note.

Because the believers are “of one heart” (v. 32), they are conscious of the needy in the church. Consequently, they help the poor among them by selling land and entrusting the proceeds to the apostles to distribute for those needs. This giving is proportional to real need. It is voluntary, not compulsory (5:4).

verse_quote: the resurrection of the Lord Jesus.
note:
The crowning proof of the salvation accomplished in Jesus Christ was His resurrection from the dead. The apostles, as chief witnesses, were especially appointed and authorized to bear eyewitness testimony about this redemptive event (1:2, 3, 8, 22; 2:32; 3:15; 4:19, 20; Luke 1:2).

**grace.** Grace in bold witnessing and generous living.
The ancient promise of covenant blessing, when Israel obeys God’s commands and cares for the poor (Deut. 15:4), is being fulfilled in the spontaneous generosity of Jesus’ followers.

In the OT, the Levites did not have inherited land, as the other tribes had, although the Levites were allotted towns (Josh. 21). However, by the time of the NT, a Levite such as Joseph Barnabas may well have been able to own land. This would have been particularly true in a country outside of Palestine, such as Cyprus, in which Joseph had grown up among the Jewish dispersion. On the other hand, the land may have belonged to his wife.

**son of encouragement.** Luke’s interpretation may be a paraphrase of the Aramaic components of the nickname that the apostles gave to Joseph, “son of a prophet”—one who speaks words of courage from God. The introduction of Barnabas here lays the foundation for further reference to the significant influence of this outstanding first-century believer in the life of the Jewish and Gentile churches and in the life of Paul. Barnabas also interceded for Saul (9:27), encouraged the church at Antioch in Syria (11:22), led in missionary work abroad (13:2, 3), and continued in missionary work despite a disagreement with Paul (15:37–39).

verse_quote: sold a field that belonged to him.
note: Joseph Barnabas presents a good example of a Christian who gives to the needs of others (contrasted with the selfish and hypocritical example of Ananias and Sapphira, 5:1–11).

verse_quote: he kept back ... some of the proceeds.
note: Ananias’s actions mimic those of Barnabas (4:36, 37) with this exception: Ananias withholds part of the sale price while claiming to contribute it all. Ananias and his wife have the right to keep all of the proceeds from their land, since the land and the money is theirs (v. 4). Their sin is in their deception (vv. 3, 4) about how much they are bringing, as Peter’s question to Sapphira implies (v. 8). The verb rendered “kept back,” which is rare in Scripture, describes the deceptive theft of Achan at Jericho (Josh. 7:1, 19–26). Here, as there, the testimony of the whole church is at risk because of the sins of a few (cf. Lev. 10:1, 2; Num. 16:23–35; 2 Sam. 6:1–7).

Another example of Satan’s influence is seen in the life of Peter (Mark 8:33). Later, Peter warns Christians against Satan’s potential influence over them (1 Pet. 5:8).

**lie to the Holy Spirit.** In v. 4 Peter tells Ananias that he has lied to God. Peter’s words indicate that the Holy Spirit is God, and that He is a divine person whose patience may be provoked, not an impersonal force (v. 9).

The instantaneous, divinely inflicted deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not typical of the miracles recorded in the NT. See the death of Herod Agrippa (12:20–23) and the temporary blinding of Saul (9:8–18) and Elymas (13:11). Some at Corinth suffered illness and even death for abusing the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:29, 30); but more typically, Christ maintains the purity of His community through the orderly process of church discipline, leading, if necessary, to excommunication (Matt. 18:15–20; 1 Cor. 5:1–5)., 10

The Holy Spirit’s presence in the Christian community brings great joy to the humble and repentant (13:52), but He is dangerous to those who prefer falsehood over transparency and truth (Heb. 12:28, 29).

**the whole church.** This is the first of more than twenty occurrences in Acts of the Greek word _ekklēsia,_ usually translated “church.” Stephen uses this word for the OT “congregation” of Israel (7:38). In the Septuagint, the worshiping assembly of God’s people is often designated with this word, and Jesus’ two uses of the term (Matt. 16:18; 18:17) imply that His community stands in continuity with and fulfillment of Israel’s calling as the Lord’s assembly. In ancient Greece, the _ekklēsia_ was the political “assembly” of citizens (19:32). The NT uses the word to refer to organized bodies of believers in one city (8:1; 13:1; 14:27), to a regional body of believers who meet in local congregations (9:31), and to the universal body of believers (Eph. 1:22, 23; 5:23, 24).

verse_quote: None of the rest dared join them.
note: In the wake of God’s judgment on Ananias and Sapphira, no insincere, superficial followers dare to identify with the church. All recognize that Christ’s Spirit imposes high standards of integrity on the holy community that He indwells.

Despite the Spirit’s dangerous holiness, new believers still came forward and join the church. Luke mentions women often in his gospel (Luke 7:28; 8:2, 3; 17:35; 23:27, 29, 49, 55) and in Acts (1:14; 8:3, 12; 9:2, 36; 13:50; 16:1, 13, 14; 17:4, 12, 34; 18:2; 21:5).

As when Jesus’ healing power flowed from His garment at the touch of the woman who had been subject to bleeding (Mark 5:27, 28), here God allows the shadow of Peter to effect a cure, as He did also through cloths and aprons that Paul had used (19:11, 12).
The exalted Lord Jesus’ exorcisms of demons and His healing acts, now through His apostles (see 1:1 note), replicate those that He performed while on earth (Luke 6:17–19).

The same Greek term describes commendable “zeal” (John 2:17), but here the Sadducean leaders of the temple are reacting from envy of the growing popular admiration (v. 13) and influence of the Christian community and the apostles (see also 13:44, 45).
See 12:6–19. Here the apostles’ release is for the sake of their ongoing, public witness in the very temple that the high priest and his colleagues control.
This aptly characterizes the gospel, since Jesus alone has the words of eternal life (John 6:68), and eternal life consists in knowing God through Him (John 17:3).

The great Jewish religious council at Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin, composed of about seventy men. It included Sadducees, Pharisees, and their associates. Under the Romans, the Sanhedrin had broad authority in Palestine. According to ancient Jewish tradition, the members sat in a semicircle with two clerks and three rows of students at the front.

It is doubly ironic that the angel of the Lord should thwart and confuse a Sanhedrin dominated by Sadducees who deny the existence of angels (23:8), and that the apostles who could not be found in the locked temple prison are preaching openly in the temple courts.

verse_quote: afraid of being stoned by the people.
note: The apostles’ popular approval, like that of their master (Luke 19:47, 48; 20:6, 19, 26; 22:2), prevents the temple authorities from harshly arresting them in public.

verse_quote: bring this man’s blood upon us.
note: In 2:23; 3:15, 16; and 4:10, 11, Peter and his associates blame the members of the Sanhedrin for the death of Jesus. The people have heard this accusation. Moreover, Jesus Himself earlier exposed the leaders’ plot to destroy Him (Luke 20:9–17); and those leaders instigated the crowds to shout, “His blood be on us and on our children” (Matt. 27:20, 25).

verse_quote: by hanging him on a tree.
note: The cruelest Roman mode of execution, crucifixion coincides with the symbolism of divine curse for the corpses of those who were executed under God’s law through Moses (Deut. 21:22, 23). Since Jesus’ resurrection demonstrates His righteousness, clearly He bore God’s curse for others’ sins, not His own (Gal. 3:13).

verse_quote: God exalted him at his right hand.
note: This declaration is understood by the Sanhedrin as a reference to the resurrection. Such an exaltation by God makes this resurrected Jesus equal with God (cf. John 5:18; 10:33).

verse_quote: we are witnesses ... so is the Holy Spirit.
note: Along with the apostles’ unique, eyewitness testimony to Jesus’ resurrection is the testimony that God’s Spirit bears to and through all who obey the call to repent and believe (Is. 59:21). Thus at Pentecost, some 120 believers, men and women, young and old, declared God’s deeds (2:4, 11, 17, 18); and soon, scattered believers (except apostles) carry the gospel outside Jerusalem, into Judea and Samaria (8:1, 4).

One of the most famous rabbis of his time, Gamaliel was Paul’s teacher (22:3) and probably a grandson of Rabbi Hillel, the leader of one of the two great schools of Jewish legal interpretation. In contrast to the school of Shammai, Gamaliel and the school of Hillel were known for their lenient interpretation of the law (Matt. 19:3 and note).

The Jewish historian Josephus (_Jewish War_ 20.118) speaks of a certain Galilean who stirred up a revolt because he resisted subservience and paying taxes to the Romans. The revolt failed, but it may have laid the groundwork for the party of the Zealots. The apostle Simon the Zealot (1:13; Matt. 10:4 and note) may have been a member of this group before becoming a disciple of Jesus.

**days of the census.** Not the census of Luke 2:1, which was ordered by the Emperor Augustus in about 8 B.C. (but was delayed until 6 or 5 B.C.), but the census fourteen years later in A.D. 6, in the time of the Procurator Coponius.
The respected Gamaliel’s counsel is far more cautious and restrained than the behavior of his disciple, Saul of Tarsus (7:58, 60; 8:3; 9:12; Gal. 1:14; Phil. 3:6; 1 Tim. 1:13).
The apostles likely receive the traditional “forty lashes less one” (2 Cor. 11:24; Deut. 25:3).

verse_quote: worthy to suffer dishonor for the name.
note: When one’s identification with Jesus’ name is the cause of ill treatment by others, such dishonor becomes, surprisingly, a privilege that imparts joy (1 Pet. 4:13–16).

The OT required care of the poor and needy (Ps. 9:18 note). This concern is seen in the social action set forth in 2:44, 45; 4:34–37. Possibly the widows among the Hellenists, that is, Greek-speaking Jews (text note), were being overlooked in the food distribution due to cultural discrimination: having resettled in Judea from the dispersion, they were considered outsiders by native-born Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking Jews. Or, since the Jerusalem church at this point numbered in the thousands and likely worshiped in home gatherings in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek), the widows’ needs taxed the distribution network beyond the capacity of the apostles to oversee it directly.

The twelve apostles including Matthias (1:26). This is a shift from “the eleven” (1:26; 2:14; Luke 24:9, 33).

**disciples.** The first of a number of times the believers are called “disciples” in Acts (e.g., v. 7; 9:1; 11:26; 13:52). Paul does not use this term to identify Christians.

**It is not right.** The high qualifications that the apostles specify (v. 3) for the men who will “serve tables” show that neither this ministry nor its recipients (Greek-speaking widows) are of minor value. The church must call others to serve these widows because the apostles’ energies cannot be deflected from their primary calling from Christ—to preach His Word.

**the word of God.** In this initial organization of the NT church, two important ministries are listed: the ministry of the Word and prayer (v. 4); and the ministry of meeting believers’ physical needs, such as serving at table. The Greek verb applied to both is _diakoneō_ (“serve”), from which the English word _deacon_ is derived. In 6:1, the related noun is translated “distribution,” and in v. 4, “the ministry.” The office of deacon, which probably had its beginning here, is described in 1 Tim. 3:8–13.

The members of the church elect the seven, and the apostles set them apart (ordained) by prayer and the laying on of hands (v. 6).

**of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom.** The two requirements for the ministry of service in all ages are dependence on and sensitivity to the Spirit and action guided by wisdom. Such qualities are discerned by others in the covenant community, who bear witness (the Greek verb _martyreõ_, “to bear witness,” lies behind “good repute”) on behalf of such leaders (Deut. 1:15; 1 Tim. 3:6, 7).

All seven men have Greek names, which may point to their being Jews from the Greek-speaking dispersion, although many first-century Palestinian Jews also had Greek names. Attributes are listed for the first and last of the seven: for Stephen (“full of faith and of the Holy Spirit”) who appears in 6:8–7:60, and for Nicolaus, “a proselyte of Antioch.” His identity as a proselyte indicates that he was born a Gentile, and subsequently converted to Judaism, presumably before coming to faith in Jesus. Antioch in Syria, third largest city of the empire (after Rome and Alexandria), will become the site of a church that welcomes Gentiles (11:19–21) and a center of missionary activity (13:1–3). Philip’s later ministry to Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch is described in ch. 8.

verse_quote: the word of God continued to increase.
note:
Because God’s Word is the source of the church’s life, Luke sums up church growth as the growth of the Word (12:24; 13:49; 19:20).

**a great many of the priests.** Priests and Levites in ancient Israel administered the distribution of resources from the tithes for the relief of widows and others in need (Deut. 14:28, 29; 26:1–4). Luke may be suggesting that as priests observed the followers of Jesus giving attention to this need, their hearts were opened to the gospel.

verse_quote: Stephen ... doing great wonders and signs.
note: Philip, another of the seven, will also perform miracles later on, like the apostles who ordained him (8:6).

Composed of Jews freed from slavery, who in this case are from Cyrene and Alexandria, well-known cities of North Africa. Such a synagogue composed of Jews from the dispersion probably conducts its meetings in Greek.

**Cilicia.** A Roman province in the southeast part of Asia Minor, with Paul’s hometown of Tarsus (9:11, 30; 11:25) as one of its chief cities. Paul (called by his Hebrew name, Saul) first appears in Acts as one who supports Stephen’s opponents (7:58, 60; 8:3). It is likely that he hears the disputations in which they cannot answer Stephen’s wisdom and the Holy Spirit (6:10).

**Asia.** The Roman province in the western part of modern-day Turkey.

These “false witnesses” (v. 13) imitate those who perjured themselves to accuse Jesus (Matt. 26:60, 61).

**blasphemous words against Moses and God.** Jesus reinforced the validity of the law that Moses had received from God and made penetrating application of its precepts, but He challenged many accretions added to the law over centuries of rabbinic tradition (Matt. 5:17–48; Mark 2:23–3:6). He also predicted the destruction of the temple (Luke 21:6). Possibly Stephen’s repetition of these teachings of his Master are deliberately misconstrued by his accusers as an assault on Moses, the lawgiver, and on God, whose presence is identified with the temple.

verse_quote: against this holy place and the law.
note: In his defense speech, Stephen does not speak directly against the temple, but only declares that God is not confined to an earthly temple since heaven is His home and throne (7:48–50). Stephen actually supports the Mosaic law and the true meaning of its teaching, which point forward to Christ (7:37, 38).

verse_quote: Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place.
note: If, in his disputation with Hellenistic Jews (vv. 9, 10), Stephen had mentioned Jesus’ statements in John 2:19 or Luke 21:6, the false witnesses misconstrued his words, since Jesus had said the Jews, not He, would destroy the temple, and He identified the temple with Himself, not a physical building (cf. Matt. 26:59–61; John 2:19–22). Stephen follows Jesus’ own views of the temple in this respect.

verse_quote: like the face of an angel.
note: If it is visibly radiant, that does not deter Stephen’s opponents from violently taking his life (7:57–60). At the least, he displays an extraordinary calm, rooted in his deep confidence in Jesus (7:55, 56).

This title recalls the divine glory God showed His people in the time of Moses: the pillar of cloud (Ex. 14:19; 16:10; Ps. 105:39), the pillar of fire (Ex. 14:24), the glory of the Lord on the mountain (Ex. 24:15–18; 2 Cor. 3:7), and the glory on the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34, 35; cf. John 1:14).

**appeared to our father Abraham ... in Mesopotamia.** Stephen’s survey of OT history highlights God’s presence with His people in locales outside the temple, Jerusalem, and the Promised Land (vv. 9, 30–34, 38, 44, 46–50).
Babylonia, in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).
Ex. 12:40 has “430,” but Stephen is speaking in round numbers, and may be following the text of Gen. 15:13, which has “four hundred years.”

God established this covenant with Abraham. He was the father of all Israel but lived centuries before Moses came. This covenant has been fulfilled in Christ, so Gentiles need not be circumcised in order to be declared righteous before God (Rom. 4).

Whereas Stephen has been accused of blaspheming Moses, history shows repeatedly that the Israelites resisted the rescuers and rulers whom God gave them: Joseph, then Moses (vv. 24–29, 35–41), the prophets (v. 52), and finally the Righteous One promised by the prophets—Jesus Himself, in whose murder Stephen’s audience is complicit (v. 52).

The Hebrew text of Ex. 1:5 has “seventy.” But the Septuagint, which this sermon is basically following, and the fragments of Exodus found among the Dead Sea Scrolls read “seventy-five.” The explanation of the “seventy-five” is to be found in the five additional descendants of Joseph included in the Septuagint’s translation of Gen. 46:20, where two sons of Manasseh, two sons of Ephraim, and one grandson of Ephraim are included.

verse_quote: the tomb that Abraham had bought ... in Shechem.
note: Stephen has condensed the events regarding the patriarchs’ burial purchases. Jacob was buried in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (Gen. 50:13), and according to Josephus (_Antiquities_ 2.199), Joseph’s brothers were buried in Hebron. Joseph’s bones, however, were placed in the land Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor (Gen. 33:19; 50:25; Ex. 13:19; Josh. 24:32). Stephen’s audience knew that Jacob and his sons were buried in two different places (Hebron and Shechem). The narrative here is highly condensed.

verse_quote: Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.
note:
Ex. 2:10 states that when the child Moses grew older, the nurse (Moses’s mother) took him to Pharaoh’s daughter and “he became her son,” with the assumption that in the royal household he would be given a full Egyptian education. Two first-century Jewish scholars, the historian Josephus and the philosopher Philo, tell of the extensive learning of Moses.

**mighty in his words and deeds.** Compare the description of Jesus in Luke 24:19.

verse_quote: He supposed that his brothers would understand.
note: Without condoning Moses’s motive and action in killing the abusive Egyptian (since Moses himself implies his cowardice in trying to evade discovery, Ex.2:11–15), Stephen directs attention to the Israelites’ defiant refusal to receive him as the means of their deliverance (vv. 26–29, 35–41).
God’s presence in the burning bush made that place in the Sinai desert holy, so to suggest that the Jerusalem temple has become obsolete (if Stephen did so) is not to blaspheme God.

Stephen does not explicitly identify Jesus as this prophet, foretold by Moses in Deut. 18:15, but Peter has made that identification (3:22) and it was implied by God’s voice at the transfiguration (Luke 9:35 note).

“Congregation” translates the Greek word _ekklēsia,_ which is used in the Septuagint to describe the assembly of Israel, gathered in God’s presence, and throughout the NT to designate the “church.” See note on 5:11.

**the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai.** Although Moses received the law from God on Mount Sinai (Ex. 20:1, 21), angels had a role in its delivery (v. 53; Deut. 33:2; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2). On the angel of the Lord, see notes on Gen. 16:7 and Judg. 2:1.

**living oracles.** God gave His law to Moses on Sinai, though the Israelites rejected both the messenger and the words that he had received through the instrumentality of angels, just as Stephen’s contemporaries are doing (v. 53).

Stephen cites Amos 5:25–27, showing that Israel’s sin with the golden calf presaged further idolatry after they entered the Promised Land. Stephen replaces Amos’s “Damascus” with “Babylon,” since the northern kingdom’s Assyrian captivity beyond Damascus was followed by Judah’s later exile in Babylon.

The OT tabernacle contained the ark of the covenant and the tablets of the Ten Commandments, which are called “the testimony.” Further symbolizing God’s presence and life-giving power were the table of the consecrated bread (Ex. 37:10–16; Heb. 9:2), the seven-branched lampstand (Ex. 37:17–23; cf. John 8:12; Rev. 1:12–18), and the altar of incense (Ex. 37:25–29), pointing to the prayers of God’s people rising up to the ever-present God (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 8:3, 4).

verse_quote: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands.
note: Solomon, who built the first temple, acknowledged that the “house” he constructed, majestic as it was, could not contain the Lord (1 Kin. 8:27). Solomon’s prayer and Isaiah’s prophecy (vv. 49, 50, citing Is. 66:1, 2) show that God’s presence cannot be confined in any physical structure, even the Jerusalem temple.

verse_quote: You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears.
note: They will not listen from their hearts, nor obey the Lord and the Scriptures Stephen has cited. These metaphors are OT figures meaning spiritually stubborn and unregenerate (Ex. 32:9; 33:3, 5; Deut. 9:6; 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; 6:10).

A title used for the Lord Almighty (Is. 24:16), for the Suffering Servant (Is. 53:11), and for Jesus Christ (3:14; 22:14; 1 John 2:1).

**you have now betrayed and murdered.** The murder of the Righteous One, for which Stephen’s hearers bear partial responsibility (2:23; 3:13–15; 4:10; 5:28), brought to a climax Israel’s rejection of God’s messengers (vv. 9, 27, 28, 35–39).

The brilliance of God’s presence (cf. Rev. 15:8; 21:11, 23).

**standing at the right hand of God.** Usually Jesus is said to be sitting at the right hand of God because His work of atonement is finished (Rom. 8:34; Col. 3:1; Heb. 10:12), but here He is standing to receive Stephen or to defend him. In this scene, the Son of Man is both Judge and Advocate.

verse_quote: I see ... the Son of Man.
note: Stephen’s vision of the Son of Man in heaven must vividly remind the Sanhedrin that when they asked Jesus, “Are you the Christ?” He replied, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:61, 62). Stephen sees the same Jesus standing in heaven at God’s right hand, proving the truth of what he was saying and condemning the Sanhedrin. Here Jesus is seen in heaven, having received the kingdom authority prophesied of the Son of Man in Dan. 7:13.

Saul, later called by his Roman name, Paul (13:9), is a Pharisee and associated with the Sanhedrin (Phil. 3:5). He may be a witness or participant in the Hellenists’ argument with Stephen and an instigator of Stephen’s trial (6:9–12; 8:3; 9:1, 2). Saul, whose sermons along with those of Peter will dominate this book, thus enters the narrative as an adamant, violent opponent of the gospel of Jesus the Christ.
As Jesus committed His spirit to his divine Father in His death (Luke 23:46; see Ps. 31:5; 1 Pet. 2:23), so Stephen commits his spirit to his divine Savior, the glorified Son.

verse_quote: do not hold this sin against them.
note: Compare the statement of Jesus in Luke 23:34 (see Luke 6:27, 28; Rom. 12:14, 17–21). The following narrative will show Stephen’s dying prayer answered in a remarkable way in the case of Saul.

verse_quote: scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.
note: For OT Israel and Judah, scattering (or dispersion) was a covenant curse resulting from their unfaithfulness to the Lord (Deut. 28:64–68; Ezek. 36:19–21), but now Stephen’s faithfulness unto death provokes the scattering of believers that spreads the good news more widely. Persecution drives the second phase and expansion of the church’s witness-bearing mission, which Jesus foretold (Acts 1:8).
The Greek verb is strong; not just harassment, but an attempt to destroy the church is meant. He arrested and imprisoned women as well as men (9:2).

Since the apostles have remained in Jerusalem (v. 1), those who now herald the good news (the Greek verb behind “preaching” here) are other believers, not Jesus’ specially designated witnesses to His resurrection (1:22). Philip, whose office focuses on mercy ministry to widows (6:2–6), is one example. Through persecution the message is spread farther and more rapidly (11:19). As the church father Tertullian said, “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.”

Samaritans, thought to be descended from intermarriage between Israel’s northern tribes and pagan peoples relocated by Assyria, revered the five books of Moses but not the rest of the OT Scriptures, and they combined devotion to idols with formalistic service to the Lord (2 Kin. 17:24–41). Relationships between Jews and Samaritans were strained at best and hostile at worst (John 4:9). Jesus reached out to Samaritans in grace, even as He categorized them as outside the covenant people (4:22; Luke 17:16, 17). By preaching Jesus as the Christ to Samaritans, Philip carries the gospel not only across geographical boundaries but also across a vast religious and racial divide.

Simon Magus the sorcerer is frequently mentioned in ancient writings outside the Bible as an archenemy of the church and one of the leaders of the Gnostic heresy. Gnosticism (named from the Greek word _gnōsis,_ meaning “knowledge”) taught that a person gained salvation not by the merit of Christ’s death for sinners, but by special knowledge about God. Justin Martyr (d. A.D. 165) says that almost all the Samaritans considered Simon the highest god (the “power of God that is called Great,” v. 10, resembling the title of a later Gnostic text). Irenaeus (d. A.D. 180), who wrote extensively against the Gnostics, regarded Simon as one of the sources of their heresies. Although the Simon of v. 9 could be another Simon, the church fathers equate the two, and the context of 8:9–11 (his character and the Samaritans’ attitude about him) permits but does not require the identification of the two as the same person.

Since Peter later states that Simon’s “heart is not right before God” and that he remains “in the bond of iniquity” (vv. 21, 23), it becomes clear that Simon’s profession of faith prior to baptism was not sincere. Luke describes Simon’s response as it first appeared to Philip and his fellow Samaritans, allowing the unfolding story to disclose the true condition of the magician’s heart.

verse_quote: receive the Holy Spirit ... they received the Holy Spirit.
note: The believing Samaritans to this point have not received observable evidence of the Holy Spirit’s gifts for ministry (v. 16), although as believers the Holy Spirit is living in them (Rom. 8:9; 1:8 note; 2:38 note). It appears that the Spirit waits to impart His extraordinary gifts so that apostles can observe and testify to the truth of the report that “Samaria had received the word of God” (v. 14), which is the second geographical area to which Acts 1:8 says the witness of the Spirit will extend (cf.10:44–46; 11:1, 12–15). This is a repeated Pentecost experience. We are not told what evidence the Holy Spirit gives of His empowering of Samaritan believers, but He manifested His arrival in some way that Simon can see and/or hear (v. 18).

verse_quote: offered them money, saying, “Give me this power.”
note: Despite his profession of faith, Simon still views supernatural power as a commodity to be purchased and controlled, and is blind to the utter graciousness of God’s gift (v. 20).

By his words and actions, Simon proves that he does not believe in Christ (v. 13 note). He is still poisoned by “bitterness” (cf. Deut. 29:18; Heb. 12:15) and “in the bond of iniquity” (see Rom. 6:16; 8:8). A profession of faith without repentance is invalid., 23

Luke does not clarify whether Simon’s plea for Peter’s intercession is a symptom of real repentance at last (as Peter commanded, v. 22) or merely an expression of terror in the face of power superior to his own. Peter has instructed Simon to pray to the Lord for forgiveness, but Luke does not record whether Simon ever does so.

From Samaria, north of Jerusalem, the Lord’s angel directs Philip southwest toward the coast, into territory once associated with Israel’s ancient enemies the Philistines (Josh. 13:1–5; Judg. 16; 1 Sam. 6:17, 18).

This word refers to either an emasculated official in the royal court (as was sometimes done to forestall temptation and corruption) or to a high official of government. Emasculation meant exclusion from Israel’s worshiping community (Deut. 23:1). Despite his political power and the great distance he had traveled, therefore, this dignitary would probably have been excluded from the temple in Jerusalem both as a Gentile and because of his physical defect.

**Candace.** The title of the queen mother who ruled in the place of her son. He was thought to be too sacred to be involved in secular affairs.

If the Ethiopian has been reading the passage about the Lord’s promise to reverse the exclusion of eunuchs and foreigners from His house (Is. 56:3–8), it would be natural for him also to read Is. 53 (v. 35 note).
In ancient times people normally read out loud.

verse_quote: told him the good news about Jesus.
note: Philip begins from Is. 53, and identifies the servant in the passage as the Suffering Servant, Jesus. Luke implies that he goes on to other OT passages to identify Jesus as the Messiah.

verse_quote: What prevents me from being baptized?
note: The eunuch’s question foreshadows that of Peter when the Gentile Cornelius and others believe and receive the Spirit (10:37), and the same Greek verb stands behind “prevents” and “withhold.”

verse_quote: the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip.
note: In Samaria an angel directed Philip to take ordinary means of travel to reach the road to Gaza, but now, in language reminiscent of Elijah (1 Kin. 18:12; 2 Kin. 2:16), the Spirit carries him to Azotus. The fact that Philip “found himself at Azotus” (v. 40) indicates that he may have been miraculously transported by the Spirit.

OT Ashdod (1 Sam. 5:1), one of the five Philistine cities, about twenty miles (32 km) north of Gaza and sixty miles (97 km) south of Caes­area on the coast. Philip preaches the gospel in all the towns along the coast until he reaches Caesarea, a large city that Herod the Great rebuilt (near Strato’s Tower). It had an excellent harbor that Herod expanded for important sea traffic (21:8), and it served as headquarters for the Roman procurators such as Pilate, Felix (23:33–24:4), and Festus (25:6). Philip must have settled in Caesarea, because years later he still resides there (21:8). His ministry along the coastal cities will blaze the trail for Peter (9:32–43).

Saul was introduced in 7:58 and he is the main character in 9:1–31. A third brief glimpse of Saul is seen again in 11:25–30 before Saul, to be called Paul as his ministry moves into the Gentile world (13:9), becomes the main character in chs. 13–28.

**still breathing threats and murder.** Saul helped to eliminate Stephen, and now he continues to persecute the Christian heresy, as he regards it (8:3). The arrests he has performed in Jerusalem and now seeks to carry out in cities of the dispersion such Damascus lead not only to imprisonment but also to death (26:10, 11).

Other names used in Acts for the early Christians are: “Christians” (used only in 11:26; 26:28; 1 Pet. 4:16), “disciples” (vv. 10, 19), “saints” (v. 13), “all who call on your name” (v. 14), and “brothers” (v. 30). “The Way” identifies the Christian cause as composed of followers of Jesus, who is “the way” (John 14:6). It is used a number of times in Acts (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22).

A supernatural light brighter than the sun (26:13) catches his attention. This is the first of three accounts of the risen Christ confronting Saul, his persecutor, on the road to Damascus. The others are spoken by Paul himself to an angry crowd in the temple courtyard (22:3–16) and to the Roman procurator Festus and King Agrippa II (26:9–18). The repetition underscores the importance of this event, which is Christ’s calling of the apostle to the Gentiles.

The repetition signifies intimate personal address (cf. Gen. 22:11; 46:2; Ex. 3:4; 1 Sam. 3:10; Luke 10:41; 22:31).

**persecuting me.** Because Jesus identifies Himself so closely with those who trust and follow Him, to persecute Jesus’ disciples is to persecute Jesus (Matt. 5:10–12; Luke 10:16; John 15:18–20). Paul will later rejoice in the privilege of sharing the sufferings of Christ (Col. 1:24).

In 22:9, Paul says that “they did not understand the voice”; the Greek word can mean “sound” or “voice.” Saul’s companions hear a sound but cannot understand what is being said.

**seeing no one.** In 22:9, Paul says his fellow-travelers “saw the light,” which he implies also in 26:13. Although they have witnessed the general radiance of Christ’s glory, they have not discerned His form. Paul’s companions can bear witness to objective audible and visible phenomena, so his experience is not merely psychological. Yet the specific content of Christ’s revelation is intelligible to Paul alone.

verse_quote: he saw nothing ... they led him by the hand.
note: Paul’s temporary blindness recalls the covenant curse that befalls Israel for their rebellion (Deut. 28:28, 29; see Is. 59:10).

Obviously not the man who was struck dead for his hypocrisy (5:1–6). Ananias of Damascus was “a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there” (22:12), as well as a believer in Jesus. This common name refers to “the Lord’s favor” and (in the form “Hananiah”) is borne by various individuals in the OT, including one of Daniel’s three friends in exile (Dan. 1:6).

**The Lord.** The One who appeared to Ananias and sent him to the blinded Saul is specifically identified as the risen Jesus (vv. 13, 17).

verse_quote: chosen instrument ... before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.
note: Paul considered himself to be an apostle to the Gentiles (Rom. 1:13, 14) as Peter was to the Jews (Gal. 2:8); but Paul also preached many times to the Jews, particularly in their synagogues (v. 20; Rom. 1:16; 1 Cor. 9:20). Acts 13–28 will show Paul proclaiming Jesus as Christ to Gentiles (ch. 13–20), kings (ch. 26), and the children of Israel (ch. 22, 28).

verse_quote: he must suffer for the sake of my name.
note: As Saul has inflicted suffering on others who trusted Christ, now he will receive such persecution as the Savior’s spokesman (2 Cor. 11:23–33). It will begin almost immediately (vv. 23, 24).

Saul has not had a dream or seen a vision, but has seen the Lord, who pressed him into service (cf. Is. 6:1, 5, 8–13).

**be filled with the Holy Spirit.** Cf. 2:38. Nothing is said about supernatural gifts such as tongues or prophecy, but emphasis is placed “immediately” on his powerful preaching about Jesus as the Son of God (v. 20).
Luke frequently calls attention to physical afflictions (13:11; 28:3–8). See Introduction: Author.

verse_quote: confounded the Jews ... by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
note: His expertise in the Scriptures now subdued and redirected by Jesus’ sovereign Spirit, Saul becomes an unanswerable advocate of Jesus’ messianic identity, as Stephen (whose martyrdom had pleased Saul) was before him (6:10; see 9:28, 29).
On this first Jewish plot on Paul’s life at Damascus and how it was thwarted, see 2 Cor. 11:32, 33.

verse_quote: when he had come to Jerusalem.
note: As Ananias was alarmed at Saul’s reputation for violence until Jesus reassured him (vv. 13–16), believers in Jerusalem suspect a ruse to infiltrate their ranks and inflict greater harm.

verse_quote: Barnabas ... brought him to the apostles.
note: Barnabas is not only generous (4:36, 37) but also ready to risk getting acquainted with a known persecutor who now claims to follow Jesus. According to Gal. 1:18, 19, Paul saw only Peter and James the Lord’s brother at Jerusalem. They may be the apostles to whom Luke refers (though James was not one of the Twelve), or else Barnabas merely introduced Saul to others, whereas Saul conferred more deeply with Peter and James.
The group who had debated with Stephen and engineered his martyrdom (6:9–14) is now silenced by Saul.
A second murder plot against Saul is foiled, and “the brothers” send him to safety in his home city in Cilicia for a time (21:39).

In another summary transition (see 2:42–47; 4:32–35; 6:7; etc.), Luke tells how, in the aftermath of Saul’s conversion, peace and growth were enjoyed by the church throughout Palestine, from Judea in the south, and Samaria in the center, to Galilee in the north.
**Peter ... came down.** In order to minister in coastal towns, following Philip’s footsteps (8:40).
The power to raise a paralyzed man or a deceased woman (v. 40) resides in Jesus, not in His servants (3:12–16).
