The news concerning the healing of the paralytic has dramatic effects; it travels to the Plain of Sharon, which extends north of Joppa up the coast forty to fifty miles (64–80 km).

An ancient seaport (modern Jaffa, south of Tel Aviv), about thirty-eight miles (61 km) northwest of Jerusalem, the port from which Jonah sailed (Jon. 1:3), and sixty-four miles (103 km) south of Caesarea Maritima, the provincial capital where Cornelius was posted (10:1).

**Tabitha.** See text note on “Dorcas_._”
Probably before the anointing with spices (cf. John 19:40). In Jerusalem, Jesus’ body was buried on the day of death, but outside the city a longer period was allowed (up to three days).

verse_quote: Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed.
note: In some ways, Peter’s actions echo those of Elijah in raising the son of the widow of Zarephath (1 Kin. 17:19–23) and of Jesus in raising Jairus’s daughter (Mark 5:40–43).

Jews believed tanning to be an unclean profession because it involved contact with dead animals (Lev. 5:2). Peter may have been willing to stay with a tanner because the message of the gospel was beginning to break down barriers between people. Even so, Peter had not yet fully grasped the implications of this principle (vv.14, 15). Peter’s stay with Simon the tanner anticipates Peter’s vision in 10:9–23.

The significance of this Roman centurion coming to faith in the crucified and risen Christ in response to the preaching of the apostle Peter is indicated by its being narrated twice (10:1–48; 11:5–17) and then mentioned by Peter a third time (15:7–9), as well as its links to the Spirit’s descent at Pentecost (10:44–47; 15:8, 9).

**10:1 Caesarea.** Caesarea Maritima was a seaport on the Mediterranean sixty-five miles (105 km) northwest of Jerusalem. It was rebuilt and improved on an ambitious scale by Herod the Great, and became the provincial capital from which Roman procurators governed Judea (23:23–35).

A term indicating that Cornelius is partly converted to Judaism, a Gentile who worships the one true God but who is not circumcised as a full proselyte (11:2, 3; contrast 2:11; 6:5). Gentiles who “feared God” (13:16, 26) were drawn to Israel’s monotheistic faith and the law’s ethical norms but did not submit to Israel’s ceremonial distinctives, which included not only circumcision but also the kosher diet and Jewish festival calendar.

**gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.** Compare another Roman centurion who was commended for generosity to the Jewish people (see 10:22) and for extraordinary faith (Luke 7:2–10).

About 3 p.m., when the evening sacrifice and special prayers are offered in the temple in Jerusalem in that day (3:1 note).

**in a vision an angel of God.** As God sent angels to appear to Zechariah and to Mary, announcing the conceptions of John the Baptist and Jesus (Luke 1:11–20, 26–38), now He sends His angel to a Gentile, directing him to an apostolic bearer of the message of salvation (Acts 10:33; 11:14).
Peter probably prayed three times a day (cf. 3:1; Dan. 6:10); this was his midday prayer. Houses typically had flat roofs reached by an outside stairway.
Peter’s consciousness is withdrawn from external things in preparation for the vision (cf. 22:17).
Both clean and unclean animals, as is shown by the mention of “reptiles” (listed as unclean “swarming things” in Lev. 11:29–31, 41–43).
The divine voice makes no distinction between living things whose meat is kosher and those that will bring ceremonial defilement.

Peter is unwilling to violate the OT laws that prohibited eating unclean animals. His words echo the protest of Ezekiel (a priest) when God commanded that he defile himself by eating bread cooked over human waste (Ezek. 4:9–14).

Through this vivid illustration, God tells Peter that He has abrogated the Mosaic regulations of ritual cleanliness. Peter will draw the valid inference that this change in the ceremonial law represents God’s intention to welcome Gentiles into His community by faith in Christ (v. 28). Jesus’ earlier teaching on the true source of defilement implied that the dietary laws would pass away (Mark 7:14–19).
The vision is repeated to demonstrate the absolute certainty of the message that it conveys and the imminence of its implementation (see Gen. 41:32).

verse_quote: some of the brothers ... accompanied him.
note: This detail is significant: when the Spirit descends on Cornelius and his Gentile associates, there will be multiple witnesses, Jewish Christians, who can confirm Peter’s account of God’s surprising action (vv. 45, 46; 11:12).
It takes the group two days to travel thirty miles (48 km) from Joppa to Caesarea.

Peter is now willing to enter the house of a Gentile (v. 28).

**fell down at his feet and worshiped him.** Cornelius is overawed at Peter’s presence; he has been instructed by God to send for the apostle, who will bring a message of salvation (11:14).
The apostles consistently refuse to accept attention or adulation that belongs only to God Himself (3:12–16; 14:15–17; see Rev. 19:10; 22:8, 9).

Peter grasps that the vision he has seen (v. 15) pertains not primarily to God’s making once-unclean foods acceptable, but to God’s cleansing people by grace alone through faith alone (15:9), apart from compliance with the dietary or other regulations of the law of Moses.
God’s impartiality, which is taught in the law (Deut. 10:17, 18), comes to its fullest expression in the gospel, which is for both Jews and Gentiles (1:8; 15:9; Rom. 1:16; 3:29, 30).

verse_quote: preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ.
note:
The peace of reconciliation with God through the blood of Jesus, our peace (Eph. 2:13, 14).

**Lord of all.** Since Jesus is Lord of both Jews and Gentiles, both receive the salvation He has achieved by faith (Rom. 10:12, 13).

verse_quote: God anointed Jesus ... with the Holy Spirit.
note: At Jesus’ baptism, the Spirit descended to empower Him for His mission as Messiah, the Anointed One (Luke 3:21; 4:1, 14, 18).
As one cursed by God, according to Deut. 21:22, 23, though the curse Jesus bore was ours (Gal. 3:13).
On Jesus’ direct choice of apostles to testify to His resurrection, see notes on 1:2, 21–25.

verse_quote: To him all the prophets bear witness.
note: Sermons earlier in Acts (2:14–36; 3:12–26) suggest some Scriptures that Peter might have begun to cite, had not the Holy Spirit’s sudden descent on his hearers intervened.

verse_quote: the Holy Spirit fell on all.
note: They are anointed by the Spirit’s power and are praising God and speaking in tongues (v. 46).

It is difficult for strict Jews who have not seen Peter’s vision to realize that God does not show favoritism in His offer of salvation.

**even on the Gentiles.** Anticipated in the conversion of the Samaritans (8:12–17) and the Ethiopian eunuch (8:26–39), the inclusion of uncircumcised Gentiles by the Spirit through faith in Jesus marks a new phase in the expansion of God’s church to embrace all the nations. It occurs through the preaching of Peter, one of Jesus’ “inner three” (with James and John) among the Twelve, and with “believers from among the circumcised” present as witnesses (11:12).

Together with v. 45 (“the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles”), this shows that the prophecy of Joel 2:28–32—a prophecy about Israel’s blessing that began to be fulfilled at Pentecost in believing Jews—is also being fulfilled in Gentiles. Thus, they also are becoming true end-time Israel in fulfilling this prophecy about Israel. This is why some Jewish bystanders are “amazed”: they see a prophecy intended for Israel being fulfilled among Gentiles. Of course, the reason for this, noted in Acts 2:17–21, is that Jesus as true Israel was the first Israelite to fulfill the Joel prophecy, and all who identify with Him become Israel, and thus fulfill the prophecy. This is still part of the second geographical area to which Acts 1:8 says the witness of the Spirit would extend (Acts 8:15–17 note). This is a repeated Pentecost experience.

Since God the Spirit Himself has signified His welcome of Cornelius and his companions into the church, no human dares deny their reception of the sign of inclusion in the community of the new covenant (11:17).

verse_quote: in the name of Jesus Christ.
note: Forgiveness of sins is through the name of Jesus, that is, through faith in Him (v. 43; 15:9, 11; see 2:38).

verse_quote: the Gentiles also had received the word of God.
note: A similar report concerning Samaria previously reached the apostles in Jerusalem (8:14), eliciting investigation by Peter and John, through whom the Holy Spirit came upon Samaritan believers, signifying their inclusion in God’s church (8:15–17).
Jewish Christians who believe that circumcision should be required for Gentiles who seek to identify with the people of God and the followers of Jesus the Messiah.

Eating with non-Jews, as Peter and his companions do “for some days” (10:48), is a clear violation of the ceremonial law because Gentiles do not follow the OT dietary laws (Lev. 11) or ceremonial washings (Mark 7:5).

As in the story of the search for Isaac’s wife (Gen. 24), Peter’s repetition of his rooftop vision and the events at Cornelius’s home reinforces the momentous significance of this event, in which God called uncircumcised Gentiles to faith in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ and gave them His Spirit.
God’s saving grace is often extended to whole families, as consistently appears in the OT (e.g., Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their families) and the New (2:38, 39; 16:31; Luke 19:9).

Before His ascension, Jesus reminded His apostles of John the Baptist’s prophecy of the baptism of the Holy Spirit (1:4, 5), which Christ accomplished at Pentecost (2:33). Peter has seen that the same “last days” gift, the Spirit, who was poured out in power on the waiting believers seven weeks after Christ’s resurrection, has now embraced Gentiles by faith in the crucified and risen Jesus.

This full title of Jesus is first used here.

**I could stand in God’s way.** It was God’s will to save both Jews and Gentiles; no doubt some of those present were reminded of God’s promise to Abraham: “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3; cf. Acts 3:25, 26; Gal. 3:8).

Although humans are responsible to turn from unbelief and sin (2:38; 3:19), only God can enliven and empower dead hearts to make that turn toward Him (3:26; 14:27; 16:14).

**repentance that leads to life.** Biblical repentance means sorrow for sin and a change of heart that turns from sin toward God (20:21). The fruits of repentance are the good works to which God calls us (26:20; Luke 3:8; Eph. 2:10).

verse_quote: scattered because of the persecution ... over Stephen.
note: As the persecution “scattered” Philip to bring the gospel to Samaria, an Ethiopian eunuch, and the Philistine coastlands (8:1, 4–40), so others traveled northwest to Antioch in Syria and the Mediterranean island of Cyprus. Antioch was a cosmopolitan city that ranked with Rome and Alexandria for cultural and commercial influence in the first century.

As the text note indicates, in contrast to the Jews to whom the scattered believers first spoke the word exclusively, “Hellenists” here designates Greek-speaking (presumably uncircumcised) Gentiles, like Cornelius and his associates down the coast in Caesarea Maritima.
The men preached, but people were saved as God called them to believe in Him (1 Cor. 3:6).

verse_quote: The report ... came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem.
note: As happened with Samaria (8:14) and Cornelius (11:1), the report of an entire church composed of Gentiles reaches Jerusalem, and Barnabas is sent to confirm the report and build up the church. He is an ideal choice as a native of Cyprus (4:36) and “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith” (11:24), like Stephen (6:5).

verse_quote: to Tarsus to look for Saul.
note: Recognizing Saul’s passion and gifts for teaching Scripture, Barnabas seeks him out in Saul’s home city in Cilicia (9:30; 21:39) and enlists him to ground new believers’ faith in the Word, launching a fruitful ministry partnership (13:2–15:35).

The word “Christian” occurs three times in the NT: here, 26:28, and 1 Pet. 4:16. It means a person belonging to or following Christ (as “Herodians” were servants or subjects of Herod, Mark 3:6). The name may have originated in the church, or it may at first have been a derogatory term used by outsiders.

Widespread, not local.

**the days of Claudius.** Claudius ruled the Empire from A.D. 41 to 54. The Nile River flooded in A.D. 45, severely reducing the Egyptian grain harvest on which the Roman Empire depended, and a severe famine struck Judea from A.D. 46 to 48.

As the church in Jerusalem had sent the church in Antioch spiritual gifts such as Barnabas, Saul, and Agabus, now this Gentile church contributes to relieve material needs of believers in Judea—an exchange that continues later in apostolic history (Rom. 15:25–27).

The first mention of this office in the history of the apostolic church. As Barnabas and Paul plant churches, they appoint elders to oversee each congregation (14:23; 20:17–35; see 15:2, 6–29). See 1 Tim. 3:1–7; 5:17–20; Titus 1:5–9.
Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and nephew of Herod Antipas, who had John beheaded (Luke 9:9; 23:7–11).
One of the three apostles closest to Jesus (along with his brother John and Peter, Luke 9:28; Mark 14:33), James is the first recorded martyr among the apostles.

verse_quote: it pleased the Jews ... arrest Peter also.
note:
God’s sovereign purpose is carried out in the lives of His equally dedicated servants: at this time, James dies by the sword, while Peter is delivered from prison.

**during the days of Unleavened Bread.** With so many zealous Jews visiting the city at the feast, it is an opportune time to make the arrest.

verse_quote: an angel of the Lord ... a light shone.
note: The angel is a messenger sent from God’s presence for Peter’s protection (Ps. 34:7), and the light probably reminds Peter of the OT glory of the Lord (9:3; Ex. 3:2; 13:22; 40:34).

verse_quote: iron gate leading into the city.
note: The Antonia Fortress had an entrance into the temple courts on the south as well as other entrances to the city.

The disciples prayed fervently to God (v. 5; cf. 4:23, 24) to protect and deliver Peter, but then failed to believe that the Lord had done what they requested.

**12:15 his angel.** They think it was his personal angelic guardian (Matt. 18:10; Heb. 1:14). The popular conception is that such a guardian can assume the appearance of the person he protects.

Not the son of Zebedee, who has been martyred (v. 2), but James the brother of the Lord Jesus, who came to faith after Jesus’ resurrection (1:14; 1 Cor. 15:7; Gal. 1:19) and is emerging as a leading elder in the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21; 21:18–26).
According to Roman law, if a prisoner escaped, the guard was liable to be punished as the prisoner would have been (cf. 16:27, 28; 27:42, 43; Matt. 28:11–15).

verse_quote: an angel of the Lord struck him.
note:
As the Lord’s angel struck Peter’s side to awaken and rescue him (v. 7), so the angel of the Lord strikes Herod in judgment, bringing about his painful death.

**did not give God the glory.** In his pride, he accepts for himself the praise that belongs to God.

**eaten by worms.** The Jewish historian Josephus records that Herod Agrippa I experienced heart pains together with pain in his abdomen and died after five days. Herod died in A.D. 44, the fourth year of Claudius Caesar.

verse_quote: Barnabas and Saul ... had completed their service.
note:
This was the mission of bringing the Antioch famine relief gift to Jerusalem (11:27–30).

**John ... Mark.** Possibly the young man who fled the night of Jesus’ arrest (Mark 14:51, 52). Mark, the writer of the second gospel (cf. 1 Pet. 5:13), accompanies Paul and Barnabas down to Antioch and goes with them on the first missionary journey (13:4) as far as Perga in Pamphylia (13:13).

See note on 4:36.

**Simeon ... called Niger.** His second name means “black” in Latin and he may have come from Africa. He may be the same as Simon of Cyrene (Luke 23:26), whose sons, Alexander and Rufus, were among the Christians at Rome (Mark 15:21; cf. Rom. 16:13).

**Lucius of Cyrene.** Cyrene was the capital of the Roman province of Cyrenaica (in modern Libya, North Africa). The ethnic variety among the church’s leadership at Antioch reflected the city’s demographic diversity.

**a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch.** Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, had beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus, but the gospel captured the heart of one of his childhood companions, whose family must have been prominent in Roman Palestine.
He probably speaks through one or more of those worshiping and fasting prophets.

They officially place their hands on Barnabas and Saul in recognition of what the Holy Spirit has already done (v. 2) and what He is going to do in sending them out (v. 4; cf. 14:23; 1 Tim. 4:14), and to symbolize the solidarity of the church and its leaders with those now sent out from their midst to carry the gospel into new regions.

The port of Antioch, sixteen miles (26 km) west of Antioch.

**Cyprus.** An island in the Eastern Mediterranean, then inhabited largely by Greeks but also by many Jews.

They have sailed directly west about 130 miles (209 km) from Seleucia to the east coast of Cyprus. Salamis is the most important city on the island in that era; the provincial capital is Paphos, ninety miles (145 km) southwest.

**the synagogues of the Jews.** In keeping with God’s covenant promises to the patriarchs, the gospel is brought “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1:16; Acts 3:26; 13:46, 47), so the missionaries’ first priority is to bring the message of Jesus to Jewish synagogues (13:14; 14:1).

**John to assist them.** See note on 12:25.
The Greek _magos_ means “wise man” (Matt. 2:1), “sorcerer,” or “magician.” Sorcery was forbidden in Judaism, but was not unknown. Bar-Jesus (“son of Joshua”) was indeed a false prophet.

Possibly Lucius Sergius Paulus, who had been an official during the reign of Claudius and then became proconsul (the chief officer in a senatorial province) at Paphos in Cyprus (cf. 18:12; 2 Cor. 9:2). By contrast, Palestine was an imperial province and had a procurator responsible directly to the emperor.

Another name for Bar-Jesus, possibly related to Semitic terms meaning “sage” or “dream interpreter.” This man is in the proconsul’s court, perhaps as an advisor valued for his presumed clairvoyance into future events. Foreshadowing future trends (vv. 45–48), this Jewish man opposes God’s Word, whereas the Gentile proconsul Paulus is eager to hear it and believe (v. 12).

“Saul” was his Jewish name and “Paul” (Latin _Paulus_) his Roman name, probably going back to his life in Tarsus. Luke uses the occasion of the conversion of a prominent Gentile official, Sergius Paulus, to introduce the familiar name of the apostle to the Gentiles. From this point on, except when Paul recounts his conversion en route to Damascus (22:7, 13; 26:14), the apostle to the Gentiles will be designated by his Roman name.

The darkness that falls on Elymas’s eyesight is temporary, as Saul’s had been (9:9). Both signs of judgment represent God’s covenant curse on rebellious Israel (Deut. 28:28, 29) and symbolize the deeper spiritual disability of unbelief (Is. 42:19–20), which can only be cured by Christ (Is. 42:6, 7).

The city of Perga was in Pamphylia, an economically poor Roman province on the south coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Perga was five miles (8 km) inland. It is at this time that John Mark leaves Paul and Barnabas and returns home for reasons that Paul deems unacceptable (15:37–39).

This Antioch was about a hundred miles (160 km) north of Perga and 3,600 feet (1,100 m) above sea level. It was in Phrygia but near Pisidia, and it was popularly called “Antioch in Pisidia” to distinguish it from another Antioch in Phrygia.

verse_quote: reading from the Law and the Prophets.
note:
A worship service in the synagogue would include the creed (Deut. 6:4), the prayer of “Eighteen Blessings,” a reading from the Law and another from the Prophets, an exposition and application (Luke 4:16–30), and a concluding benediction.

**word of encouragement.** A spoken discourse explaining the meaning and relevance of one or more of the Scriptures that was read aloud. The author to the Hebrews calls that entire work a “word of encouragement” (Heb. 13:22).

Although Saul (Paul) had spoken of Christ in Damascus, Jerusalem, Antioch, and Cyprus, this is the first sample of his preaching included in Acts. Like Peter’s sermon at Pentecost, it shows Jesus’ tie to David, quotes and explains Ps. 16 (as well as other Scriptures), and describes both Jesus’ undeserved suffering at human hands and His resurrection by God’s power, ending with a promise of forgiveness to those who believe.
About four hundred years plus the forty years in the wilderness and the period of Joshua’s conquest (7:6 note).

verse_quote: for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him ... who are now his witnesses to the people.
note: Paul and Barnabas bring the same good news (v. 32) to their hearers in the dispersion that the original apostles are proclaiming in Judea, but the latter have a distinctive role as witnesses, since they accompanied Jesus during His ministry and saw Him repeatedly between His resurrection and ascension (1:3–8, 22; 2:32; 5:32).

verse_quote: You are my Son, today I have begotten you.
note: That is, “Today in raising You from the dead, I am declaring that You are My Son and I am Your Father” (Heb. 1:5 note).

verse_quote: no more to return to corruption.
note: That is, never to die again, unlike David himself (vv. 36, 37), who did not personally receive “the holy and sure blessings” promised to him (citing Is. 55:3) but predicted their arrival in his messianic descendant, Jesus.

The law points the sinner to Christ (Gal. 3:24), for “a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 2:16). To be justified is to be declared righteous by God (Rom. 3:21, 22), and therefore granted forgiveness of sins (Eph. 1:7). See theological note “Justification by Faith” on p. 2078.

verse_quote: many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas.
note: Many, both ethnic Jews and Gentile proselytes, heed the missionaries’ promise of forgiveness (vv. 38, 39) and their sober warning against scoffing unbelief from Hab. 1:5 (v. 41). On the next Sabbath, the hostile reaction of unbelieving Jews reveals how apt the warning was (v. 45).

Jews who have rejected the message about Jesus resent its popularity among the city’s Gentiles (and other Jews), as jealousy has moved the high priest and other Sadducees to oppose the apostles in Jerusalem (5:17).

verse_quote: the word of God ... first to you.
note: Since Jesus the Messiah came through the Jews (Gen. 12:3), Paul is consistent in applying the principle “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1:16). He recognizes that God’s plan also includes the Gentiles (Is. 49:6), a fact resisted by these Jews of Pisidian Antioch.

God’s word to His servant, cited here from Is. 49:6, applies first of all to Jesus, as the aged prophet Simeon recognized (Luke 2:30–32). Yet Jesus, who is the light to the Gentiles and of the world (John 8:12) also commissions His followers to reflect His light to others as “the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Christ alluded to this prophecy in His promise that they would be His witnesses “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Paul and his colleagues thus also fulfill the Is. 49:6 prophecy, first fulfilled by Jesus (Luke 2:32; Acts 26:23), because they are identified with Him by corporate solidarity. They are “apostles” in Christ and, therefore, participate in His commission given in Is. 49:6.

verse_quote: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
note: God chose these people beforehand (in eternity past), and now through giving them repentance (11:18; 2 Tim. 2:25) has brought them to faith in Christ (Eph. 2:8). Luke uses the passive voice (“were appointed”), indicating that God is the agent. Only God grants eternal life (Matt. 25:46; John 10:28; 17:2). See theological note “Predestination and Reprobation” on p. 1997.

verse_quote: shook off the dust from their feet.
note: A Jewish sign of repudiation and disassociation (Matt. 10:14).

verse_quote: filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
note: Joy is the Spirit’s fruit in believers’ lives (8:39; Gal. 5:22; Rom. 14:17; 15:13; 1 Thess. 1:6).

Paul and Barnabas have traveled eighty miles (129 km) southeast from Antioch in Pisidia to Iconium, an ancient Phrygian town. The Greeks made it a city-state, and under Augustus it became a city in the province of Galatia.

For the first time in Acts, the term has a broader reference that includes men such as Barnabas in addition to the apostles chosen by Jesus (1:24–26; cf. Matt. 10:1–4; 2 Cor. 1:1 note). The term “apostle” means “one sent,” with the connotation of bearing authority, so it is applied elsewhere in the NT to other individuals (2 Cor. 8:23) besides the Twelve and Paul, whom Jesus appointed apostle to the Gentiles on the Damascus Road (Rom. 11:13; Gal. 1:1).
Stoning was the way ancient Jews executed the death penalty for blasphemy against God (7:58, 59; cf. Lev. 24:13–16).

These two cities along with Iconium belonged strictly to the Roman province of Galatia, although they were part of the subdistrict called Lycaonia. From A.D. 37–72 Iconium was linguistically and politically on the Phrygian side of the border.

In 6 B.C., Augustus fortified this settlement and made it into a Roman colony of the province of Galatia. He also settled the colony with Roman army veterans. Returning to Lystra on a second journey, Paul would recruit a young believer named Timothy to join his missionary team (16:1–3). Perhaps it was during this first visit of Paul and Barnabas that Timothy and his Jewish mother and grandmother came to believe in Jesus as the Messiah promised in the OT (2 Tim. 1:5; 3:10, 11, 14, 15).

verse_quote: he sprang up and began walking.
note: This healing, like that in the Jerusalem temple through Peter and John (3:1–4:22), enables a man crippled from birth to both walk and leap. Both miracles attracted the crowds’ attention to the apostles, who hasten to direct glory away from themselves to God. See theological note “Miracles” on p. 532.

An ancient legend circulated in Lystra that the Greek gods Zeus and Hermes disguised themselves as men and came to the Phrygian hill country, seeking hospitality. Only one couple welcomed them, and in return their cottage was changed into a temple with a golden roof and marble columns. The houses of those who refused the gods were destroyed. The Lystrans may have been thinking of this legend when they welcomed Barnabas and Paul and prepared to sacrifice oxen, mistaking them for those gods, revisiting the region incognito.. 13
A conventional sign of grief or distress (Mark 14:63).

The content of Paul’s sermon is similar to his later sermon at Athens (17:22–31). Both sermons are addressed to pagan crowds who would not understand quotations from and explanations of OT Scriptures. Paul stresses that God’s creative and providential power extends everywhere. See Rom. 1:18–23. See theological note “Divine Revelation” on p. 850.
When addressing the philosophers in Athens, Paul calls the era before Christ’s coming “the times of ignorance” (17:30).
A Lycaonian border town in southeastern Galatia, sixty-five miles (105 km) southeast of Lystra.

As Jesus called those who would follow Him to count the cost and expect persecution (Matt. 5:10–12; Luke 9:23–26; John 15:20), so the apostles bluntly prepare believers to expect suffering along the path that leads to glory (Phil. 3:10, 11; 2 Tim. 2:11, 12; 3:12; 1 Pet. 4:10–19).

Elders governed ancient Israel’s tribes (Num. 11:16–30; Deut. 1:9–18) and had a similar role in first-century Judaism (Luke 7:3; 22:66). So also, each of the congregations in the apostolic church was led by elders, men recognized for wisdom and mature character (11:30; Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9; 1 Pet. 5:1–4).

The reports of Paul’s and Barnabas’ direct contact with the Gentiles on the first missionary journey may have reached Judea and Jerusalem through John Mark after he returned home (13:13). Also, others from Syrian Antioch may have brought the news during Paul and Barnabas’ extended stay there. This seems to have caused some Jewish Christians to fear that their Jewish heritage was threatened; they thought that the converted Gentiles must be brought into Judaism through circumcision, and that full compliance with the law of Moses was required in order to merit salvation (vv. 1, 5). Paul recognized that forcing Gentiles to be circumcised might make them think that salvation must be earned through keeping God’s law (cf. Gal. 2:15, 16). He knew that the Judaizers had to be opposed lest their teaching obscure the freedom of God’s grace and the sufficiency of Christ’s cross and righteousness (Gal. 2:20, 21; Phil. 3:9), and thereby hinder the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles (1 Thess. 2:14–16).

verse_quote: to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders.
note: Because the issue has great significance for the clarity of the gospel and the unity of the church, when it could not be resolved in Antioch, it is referred to a wider circle of leaders, the apostles and elders of the “mother church” in Jerusalem.

verse_quote: apostles and the elders were gathered together.
note: The church leaders take the lead in the discussion, but v. 12 indicates that the whole assembly is present.

Peter recounts the events surrounding Cornelius, noting specifically that God gave that centurion and his Gentile associates the Holy Spirit without their receiving circumcision, thereby demonstrating that He had “cleansed their hearts by faith” (v. 9) and saved them “through the grace of the Lord Jesus” (v. 11), just as Jewish believers had been saved.

verse_quote: a yoke on the neck of the disciples.
note: The rabbis spoke of a person’s commitment to submit to God’s law using the imagery of a yoke, the farm implement by which oxen were bound to pull a plow. Peter reminds his fellow Jews that they themselves have been unable to fulfill the law with the perfection required if their obedience were the condition of God’s acceptance (Gal. 5:1). They have been “saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus,” which means they have been “freed from” the unbearable burden of the law by Jesus’ death and resurrection (Acts 13:39).

James is the half-brother of Jesus (12:17; Matt. 13:55; Gal. 2:9; 1 Cor. 15:7; Introduction to James: Author). He seems by now to be a prominent leader of the Jerusalem church (21:18). James adds a third testimony that Gentile believers should not be burdened with keeping the details of the Jewish ceremonial law; his speech places the reports of Peter, Barnabas, and Paul in the context of the Scriptures, showing how the OT foretold that God would take the Gentiles as “a people for his name” (v. 14), in fulfillment of Amos 9:11, 12 (v. 17).
The resurrection of Jesus, David’s messianic descendant, and His enthronement in heaven fulfilled God’s promise to establish David’s dynasty eternally (2:25–36; 13:22, 23).

James finds support in the Scriptures and in the testimonies of Simon Peter, Barnabas, and Paul that God wants the Gentiles to be free from the ceremonial law and the demands of the Judaizers. He proposes that both Jews and Gentiles practice moderation. The Jewish Christians are to recognize that Gentiles are not to be bound by Jewish ceremonial law. The Gentile believers must consider the scruples of Jewish Christians and not offend them by eating food sacrificed to idols, the meat of strangled animals, or blood (Lev. 17:10–14; 19:26). The inclusion of “sexual immorality” (a moral, not ceremonial, requirement) along with these dietary restrictions may indicate that all four practices from which Gentile Christians are to abstain relate to idolatrous pagan worship practices. However, the witness of the NT as a whole indicates that sexually immoral behavior is still off limits for Christians even in cases where it is not associated overtly with pagan worship (Matt. 5:27–30; 1 Cor. 5; 6:9).
Judas and Silas, who are prophets (v. 32), are sent by the council of apostles and elders to reinforce and clarify in person the meaning and implications of the council’s written letter.

The Jewish Christians use this expression to set the Gentile Christians at ease, as does the letter’s commendation of “our beloved Barnabas and Paul” (vv. 25–26), who have defended the Gentiles’ freedom from the imposition of circumcision and the many ceremonial regulations of the law of Moses.

verse_quote: to the Holy Spirit and to us.
note: They are filled with the Spirit (2:1–41; 4:8; 6:5; 9:17; 13:4) and recognize the Spirit’s role in their debate and decision.

Clearly, the Gentile Christians in Antioch do not interpret the restraint urged by the letter, following James’s counsel (vv. 20, 28, 29), as an imposition of legal demands that compromise the graciousness of the gospel in any way.
Bringing encouragement and strength to believers was a primary function of the NT prophet (a spokesman for God).

Although they have stood together in defense of the gospel and the Gentiles’ freedom, Paul and Barnabas sharply differ either over the seriousness of John Mark’s defection in Pamphylia (13:13) or on whether Mark, having repented, has matured enough to be trusted as an aide for their next journey. True to his character throughout Acts, Barnabas believes that Mark is “salvageable” for gospel service, and so he is ready to risk enlisting Mark again. Though the remainder of Acts contains no further record of Paul’s working with Barnabas, Paul mentions Barnabas in a positive light in 1 Cor. 9:6. Paul’s later high regard for Mark—in part the fruit of Bar­nabas’ mentoring—is evident in Col. 4:10; Philem. 24; 2 Tim. 4:11; cf. 1 Pet. 5:13.

**Barnabas took Mark ... Cyprus.** Barnabas takes his cousin Mark (Col. 4:10) on a missionary journey to the island of Cyprus, Barnabas’ home. This will also provide an opportunity for Barnabas to encourage (4:36) the younger man.

Paul’s new colleague is one of the prophets sent by the council in Jerusalem to explain its letter and encourage the Gentile believers in Syrian Antioch. They set off over land to the north and west, traveling through Syria and Cilicia, Paul’s home province (v. 41), en route to the interior cities of Galatia (16:1), in which Paul and Barnabas planted churches on their first trip to the region.

In the small Jewish community of Lystra, Paul finds this young man, part Jew and part Greek. Like his father, Timothy has been reared as a Greek, and so has not been circumcised. His mother is Jewish.

Although Paul adamantly resists the imposition of circumcision on Gentiles such as Titus (Gal. 2:3), Timothy’s status as the offspring of a covenantally mixed marriage (v. 1) would be questionable in the eyes of the Jewish community. Rather than risking a hindrance to Timothy’s ministry among those who might regard him as an uncircumcised Jew, Paul removes that obstacle (see 1 Cor. 9:19–23; 10:32, 33).

verse_quote: they delivered to them for observance the decisions.
note: The unity of the visible church is evident in the fact that a decision reached by a council in Jerusalem, in response to an issue in Syrian Antioch, is now communicated as binding on churches in other cities and regions.

This was the southern part of the larger Roman province of Galatia. It included the Phrygian district, Antioch of Pisidia, and the surrounding area.

**Holy Spirit ... Asia.** The Roman province of Asia, located in the western sector of Asia Minor, included the famous city of Ephesus where God wanted Paul to go at a later date (ch. 19). The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Jesus (v. 7), and He is God (v. 10; 5:3, 4; cf. 2 Cor. 3:17 note). These verses point to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity (cf. 2 Cor. 13:14).

Paul and Silas have come from Derbe and Lystra northwest to Mysia, a region to the south of the Hellespont, but the Spirit who forbade them from moving west into Asia also forbids traveling north into Bithynia. Instead, they go west to Troas, a seaport on the Aegean Sea., 8

Compare the visions by which the Lord brought Ananias to minister to the blinded Saul (9:10, 12) and Peter to preach to the centurion Cornelius (10:3, 17, 19; 11:5).

**Macedonia.** Macedonia was across the Aegean Sea from Troas.

The first of several passages (16:10–17; 20:5–15; 21:1–18; 27:1–28:16) using the plural pronoun “we” starts here, indicating that the author of Acts is traveling with Paul and Silas at this point in their ministry.
A prominent island in the north Aegean where vessels regularly stopped.

Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, had established a large Greek colony here and named it Philippi.

**a Roman colony.** This status, bestowed on Philippi by Octavian (to become Caesar Augustus) and Marc Antony, meant that Philippi’s citizens had Roman citizenship and its privileges, including due process in Roman courts and exemption from taxation.

According to later Jewish practice, at least ten men were required to form a synagogue. Failing that, a place of prayer could be established outdoors, preferably near water. Although various local and imported pagan religions flourished in Philippi, the city likely had no Jewish synagogue for instruction in Israel’s Scriptures and prayer to the true and living God.

**women who had come together.** They are meeting to read and study the Scriptures, and they welcome the assistance of any Jewish teacher who happens to visit there.

Southeast of Pergamum and about forty miles (64 km) inland, Thyatira was in Asia Minor, across the Aegean Sea from Athens. Thyatira was known for wool and dyeing. Purple was an expensive dye. Lydia apparently has the means to maintain a home large enough to accommodate Paul’s team, which includes at least Silas, Timothy, and Luke, and perhaps the church’s gatherings (v. 40). Her “household” probably includes servants (v. 15).

**a worshiper of God.** A Gentile who embraced Israel’s monotheistic faith and the law’s moral norms but did not fully convert to Judaism with respect to dietary and other ceremonial rules. See 10:2.

**The Lord opened her heart.** Divine illumination and persuasion is necessary for the heart blinded by sin to respond to the gospel (Jer. 13:23; John 6:44, 65; Rom. 9:16; 1 Cor. 2:14). This effectual call of God ensures that all who have been chosen by God will believe (11:18; 13:48; 14:27; 2 Thess. 2:13, 14; 2 Tim. 1:9, 10).

verse_quote: she was baptized, and her household as well.
note: Throughout redemptive history, God’s dealings often include entire households, acknowledging family solidarity (2:38, 39; 11:14; 16:31; cf. Gen. 17:7–14). The household baptisms of Acts are striking examples of this (10:47, 48; 16:31–33; cf. 1 Cor. 1:16). Such household baptisms were apparently standard practice in the apostolic era. Assuming that these households included infants, the baptism of entire households is indirect evidence for the practice of infant baptism.

Lit. “a python spirit.” The term originally referred to a mythical serpent believed to guard the temple and oracle of the Greek god Apollo at Delphi. Later the phrase meant a demon-possessed person or even a ventriloquist. The people at Philippi must have thought of her as having a demon that could tell fortunes.
A Jew would understand this to be Yahweh; a Gentile would apply it to Zeus.

verse_quote: name of Jesus Christ to come out.
note: As Jesus silenced demons rather that accepting their “endorsement” (Mark 1:34), so Paul is “annoyed” by the publicity that the evil spirit is offering through the girl. Following the common understanding of the expression “the Most High God,” everyone would realize that Paul means to convey the thought that Jesus, as deity, expelled the demon. A subsequent incident in Ephesus shows that Paul has authority to invoke Jesus’ name because he actually trusts in Jesus (19:13–17).

verse_quote: their hope of gain was gone.
note:
Like the silversmiths of Ephesus (19:23–28), the girls’ owners are driven by greed but conceal their true motive behind a veneer of civic pride, invoking their Roman citizenship (v. 21).

**seized Paul and Silas.** Because both Paul and Silas are Jews and the leaders of the missionary team, they are seized. Their companions are Gentiles (Luke, a Gentile from Syrian Antioch, and Timothy, a half-Gentile from Lystra) and are not charged.

verse_quote: advocate customs ... not lawful for us ... Romans.
note: The charge is that Paul and Silas are propagating an illegal religion and disturbing the peace. Because of Philippi’s status as a colony, its citizens are Romans who enjoy legal status beyond those of other Macedonian cities. The charge is inflamed by cultural and religious prejudice (“these men are Jews”). Ironically, it will come to light that Paul and Silas themselves are Roman citizens whose civic rights are being violated (vv. 37, 38).
Paul and Silas are Roman citizens (v. 37) and should be exempt from such treatment. But in the mob atmosphere, the question of their citizenship status and legal rights is ignored.
They are treated like criminals.
Paul will later remind the Philippians of this suffering and his joyful response (Phil. 1:18, 29, 30).
Earthquakes accompanied Jesus’ death and resurrection (Matt. 27:54; 28:2), as well as the outpouring of the Spirit on believers on one occasion (Acts 4:31).

On earlier occasions, God’s angel led His messengers out of prisons (5:19; 12:10); but here not only Paul and Silas but also their fellow prisoners, who have heard their prayer and praises (v. 25), remained in their cells (v. 28).

**about to kill himself.** Under Roman law, the jailer is liable to punishment if his prisoners escape (12:19; 27:42).

Throughout Acts (and the whole NT) the message is consistent: Salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ alone (2:38; 3:16; 10:43; 13:39; 15:9–11).

**you and your household.** For other instances of household salvation, see note on v. 15 note; cf. 2:38, 39; 10:24, 48; 1 Cor. 1:16. Because the head of the household has come to faith in Christ, the whole family is baptized (vv. 33, 34).

verse_quote: washed their wounds ... set food before them.
note: As Lydia’s faith led her to insist on providing hospitality to the missionaries (v. 15), so the jailor’s faith and repentance bear immediate fruit in his deeds of compassion for prisoners whom he previously handled with indifference at best. See theological note “Baptism” on p. 1988., 34

Roman citizens were exempted from scourging and torture, and had the right to due process in a trial before any punishment was inflicted. If Roman citizens were tried in a Roman court, they had the right to appeal their case to Caesar (25:11; 26:32).

Paul’s insistence on a public apology from the magistrates (v. 37) is motivated not by a sense of personal insult but by a desire to rehabilitate the gospel’s reputation in Philippi, refuting the slander that it advocates practices unfit for Romans (v. 21).

Early Christians often met in private homes (Philem. 2), and the mention of “the brothers” here suggests that Lydia was hostess to the gatherings of this young congregation.

**seen the brothers.** “Brothers” would include all the believers—Lydia, her household, the jailer, perhaps other women at the river bank, and the others who responded to Paul’s and Silas’s preaching.

Amphipolis was thirty miles (48 km) southwest of Philippi and Apollonia twenty-five miles (40 km) farther on the highway to Thessalonica. Paul and his companions were eager to get to Thessalonica, forty miles (64 km) beyond Apollonia. Thessalonica had a population of two hundred thousand and was the provincial capital of Macedonia.

The Pauline Epistles suggest that Paul stayed in Thessalonica longer than three or four weeks (including the workdays before, between, and following three successive Sabbaths). According to Phil. 4:16, the church at Philippi sent him aid at least twice, and the Thessalonian epistles indicate that Paul had been able to give extensive doctrinal instruction to the Christians there. Acts does not state that the uproar surrounding Jason, the missionaries’ host (v. 5), occurred _immediately_ after Paul’s third Sabbath of teaching in the synagogue. The conversions listed in v. 4 may have occurred over subsequent weeks, leading eventually to the hardening of Jewish opposition and the mob violence against Jason and other brothers.

verse_quote: necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise.
note: Neither Jesus’ disciples nor their Jewish hearers readily accepted the divine necessity of the Messiah’s suffering (Luke 9:43–45; 18:31–34; 24:25, 26; 1 Cor. 1:18–25). When Paul establishes this point from the Scriptures and identifies Jesus as this suffering and triumphant Messiah, some of those who attend the synagogue, both Jews and Gentile God-fearers, as well as some of “the leading women,” come to believe in Jesus (v. 4).

Paul proclaims Jesus as the anointed King who has inaugurated the spiritual kingdom of God (14:22; 19:8; 20:25; 28:23, 31), but his opponents distort Paul’s message, alleging that the apostle advocates political insurrection against Rome. About this time, Claudius Caesar (A.D. 49–50) expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2) because of riots allegedly instigated by “Chrestus,” a probable reference to disputes within the capital’s Jewish community over the identity of the Christ.
Modern Verria, fifty miles (80 km) southwest of Thessalonica, in the foothills of the Olympian Mountains.
The Bereans give Paul’s teaching an open hearing and compare it with God’s written Word. Because of their integrity and discernment, many of them come to faith in Jesus the Christ.

The leading city of Greece, served by the port of Piraeus on the Aegean Sea. Athens reached its zenith in the fifth century B.C. under Pericles (495–429 B.C.), when the Parthenon and other magnificent structures were built. The classical poets Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes flourished at that time. Although conquered by the Romans in 146 B.C., Athens continued to be a great intellectual and cultural center.

**full of idols.** There were statues of gods or goddesses in the Parthenon and other temples on the Acropolis, as well as in the public, commercial, and temple buildings below.

Epicurus (342–270 B.C.) taught that the purpose of life was pleasure and freedom from pain, passions, and fears. On the other hand, the Cypriot Zeno (340–265 B.C.), founder of Stoicism, stressed living in harmony with nature and depending on reason and other self-sufficient powers. Both schools stressed the quest for peace of mind. Zeno viewed God pantheistically as the “world-soul.”

**babbler.** A derogatory term meaning a scrap collector or peddler of assorted ideas.

**foreign divinities.** The Greek word for “resurrection” (_anastasia_) is feminine in gender, and Athenian polytheists would be familiar with the personification of abstract qualities as though divine. Perhaps Paul’s hearers confuse his declaration of an event (Jesus’ resurrection from the dead) with a female deity. That these “divinities” originate outside Athens and Achaia would devalue them in the opinion of Athens’s intellectual elite.

The name means “Mars Hill.” This is a hill near the Acropolis where in ancient times a council had met. The council became the city council of Athens, and in Roman times it was the court supervising morals, education, and religion. In Paul’s time, the court meets in the Royal Portico, in the marketplace below the Acropolis. Probably the purpose of Paul’s hearing before the council is not only to satisfy its members’ curiosity (v. 21) but also to evaluate the strange ideas that he is propagating.

The term is ambiguous, in some contexts having a negative connotation (“superstitious,” as in KJV) and in others referring more neutrally to pious devotion to deities. Without endorsing the city-wide idolatry that has so distressed him, the apostle opens his discourse by acknowledging the abundant evidence of the Athenians’ deep desire to honor those superhuman powers that, they believe, influence their destinies.

Possibly a reference to the Altar of the Twelve Gods at Athens, erected to ensure that no god is left out of their worship. Paul uses this point of contact to begin his discourse about the God who made the world, who is not carved out of stone or confined to any temple, and who controls the times and places where people live.

verse_quote: The God who made the world.
note: Epicureans conceived of the gods as remote, uninvolved in human affairs. Stoics conceived of the divine as a principle of reason that permeates the cosmos. Paul proclaims the God who is distinct from and transcendent over the universe (unlike Stoicism), but also (unlike Epicureanism) deeply engaged with His creatures, giving “to all mankind life and breath and everything” (v. 25) and assigning each nationality’s time and place (v. 26; see Deut. 32:8, 9).

The whole human race descends from Adam, its original covenant representative, whose decision affects all his naturally conceived descendants (Rom. 5:12–21; 1 Cor. 15:21, 22). See theological note “Original Sin” on p. 17.

verse_quote: seek God ... perhaps feel their way ... and find him.
note: Elsewhere, Paul (echoing Ps. 14:1–3) bluntly diagnoses the innate rebellion of the whole human race apart from God’s renewing grace: “No one seeks for God. All have turned aside” (Rom. 3:11, 12). To the Athenian philosophers, Paul’s point is that God’s general revelation makes the Gentiles’ worship of false gods inexcusable. God’s gift to all mankind of “life and breath and everything” (v. 25) should lead the whole human race to long to know their Creator. They cannot excuse their idolatries by alleging that His revelation in the created universe is insufficient, since “he is actually not far from each one of us” in that general revelation, as even pagan poets have recognized (v. 28).

verse_quote: In him we live and move and have our being.
note:
Citing a seventh-century B.C. poet (see text note), Paul says that God brought all people into being and they only exist by His providence. In the ancient world, the three great mysteries of philosophy and science were the questions of life, motion, and being. See theological note “Divine Revelation” on p. 850.

**some of your own poets.** Knowing that the Athenians do not know or respect the OT, Paul quotes from three of their own poets. Although their words originally referred to Zeus, the head of the Greek pantheon, whom Stoics reinterpreted as a personification of reason, Paul applies the quotations to the true and living God of heaven. The poets are Epimenides (c. 600 B.C.), Cleanthes (c. 331–233 B.C.), and Aratus (c. 315–240 B.C.).

Epicureans and Stoics would agree, at least implicitly, with Paul’s critique of crass popular idolatry that equates “the divine being” with material images, though they themselves have formed misconceptions of the Creator by the “imagination of man.” See theological note “The Self-Existence of God” on p. 938.

Until the coming of Jesus Christ, God’s special, redemptive revelation was addressed almost exclusively to Israel, leaving the pagan nations largely in ignorance (except for the general revelation throughout the cosmos that left them without excuse; Rom. 1:18–25). God did not impose on the Gentiles the judgment they deserved, and now He has sent Paul to proclaim His truth to all people everywhere, calling them to repentance.

verse_quote: a day on which he will judge ... by a man whom he has appointed.
note: The final day of judgment (Rev. 20:12–15) would be an alien idea both to Epicureans, who believe that the gods could not be bothered by earthly events, and to Stoics, who view history as running in endless cycles. Yet the Athenians’ rejection of the Man whom God appointed will result in Jesus’ finally and justly rejecting them on that day of judgment. Paul stresses that God’s call to repentance and faith is not merely an invitation but a command.

Some Greek philosophical schools viewed embodied life as undesirable, so they would consider absurd Paul’s claim that the One who would judge everyone was designated by God through resurrection from the dead. Others perhaps dismiss Paul’s focus on concrete historical events—resurrection and last judgment—from other philosophical or personal motives. Nonetheless, Paul’s witness to the philosophers bears fruit in the lives of some, two of whom are named: Dionysus and Damaris (v. 34).

Since 27 B.C., this city had been the capital of the Roman province of Achaia. It was fifty miles (80 km) southwest of Athens, near the isthmus that joins Attica and the Peloponnesus. Corinth was large and prosperous in the eighth to sixth centuries B.C., but it declined and was captured in 338 B.C. by Philip II of Macedon. In 196 B.C., it was taken by the Romans. They sacked it in 146 B.C. as punishment for a revolt, but it was restored by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 B.C. In NT times, Corinth had more than two hundred thousand inhabitants, including Greeks, freedmen from Italy, Roman army veterans, businessmen, government officials, people from the Near East, a large number of Jews, and many slaves. Corinth was thoroughly pagan and immoral. The city was filled with pagan temples and on the south there was a high acropolis with a temple of Aphrodite. From the fifth century B.C., the expression “to Corinthianize” meant to engage in sexual immorality.

verse_quote: Aquila, a native of Pontus ... Priscilla.
note:
Pontus was on the north coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Priscilla is frequently listed before her husband (vv. 18, 19, 26; Rom. 16:3; 2 Tim. 4:19). She may have had higher social status or have been more prominent in their tent–making business. This Jewish-Christian couple is noteworthy for their hospitality, opening their homes in Corinth, Ephesus, and Rome (to which they eventually returned) to the church’s meetings and leaders (Acts 18:24–26; Rom. 16:3–5; 1 Cor. 16:19).

**Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome.** See note on 17:7.

Like Aquila and Priscilla, Paul was a tentmaker by trade. His frequent practice was to support himself and his team through this work rather than expecting financial compensation from those whom he was evangelizing (20:33–35; 1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:7–9), although he gratefully received donations from established churches for the sake of further outreach. See note on 18:5.

verse_quote: Silas and Timothy arrived ... Paul was occupied with the word.
note: Apparently, Paul’s colleagues have brought a contribution from one or more Macedonian churches, allowing him to reduce his hours making tents and devote weekdays as well as Sabbaths to proclaiming Christ’s Word (2 Cor. 11:7–9; Phil. 4:10–20).

verse_quote: Your blood be on your own heads.
note: They are responsible for their own sins. See 20:26; Ezek. 3:16–21.

The first home of the Corinthian church. Titius Justus is a Gentile adherent to the faith at the synagogue, and a Roman citizen. He may belong to one of the families Julius Caesar sent to colonize Corinth. It is also possible that he is the Gaius of Rom. 16:23, who was baptized by Paul (1 Cor. 1:14); Gaius could be a third name standing before Titius Justus.

verse_quote: Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue.
note:
As synagogue ruler, Crispus is in charge of the physical arrangements for the synagogue services. It is this Crispus (and presumably his household) whom Paul baptizes (1 Cor. 1:14).

**his entire household.** See 16:15 and note; 16:31–33.

verse_quote: I have many in this city.
note: Jesus promises that Paul’s labors in Corinth will be fruitful because many people whom God has appointed to eternal life (13:48) and given to the Son (John 17:6) live in that city. Even though the elect Corinthians have not yet believed the gospel, they nevertheless are known to God.

verse_quote: when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia.
note: Luke’s identification of the administrative head of this senatorial province as a proconsul is confirmed by an inscription found at Delphi, Greece, which identifies Gallio as the proconsul in A.D. 52.

The Jewish accusation is ambiguous. Roman law at the time forbids the practice of religions not legally recognized by Rome. Judaism is legally recognized in the first-century Roman Empire (Latin: _religio licita_), so perhaps the opponents claim that the faith that Paul is preaching is not an offshoot of Judaism and has no claim to legitimacy before the Empire. Gallio, however, views the issue as a dispute among Jews over “your own law” (v. 15)—the law of Moses—and refuses to get involved in an intramural religious argument among the Jewish people.

Though this phrase could apply to Aquila, it is probably Paul who is in view. The Nazirite vow requires rigorous ceremonial purity that are impractical in Gentile lands (Num. 6:1–21), so this vow is more likely a private one undertaken by Paul as a religious exercise. The hair is allowed to grow during the period of the vow, and cutting it marks the conclusion of the vow and is perhaps an expression of gratitude to God (21:23, 24). Paul’s vow shows that, despite the accusations that jealous Jewish leaders have brought to the proconsul, he exercises his Christian freedom by occasionally observing Mosaic ceremonial ordinances even as he brings God’s good news to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:19–23).

Although previously prevented by the Holy Spirit from evangelizing this major city in the province of Asia, Paul now preaches Christ in the synagogue, anticipating a longer ministry to come “if God wills” (v. 21). See ch. 19, 20.

Paul is in Antioch for several months, from about autumn of A.D. 52 to spring of A.D. 53.

**Galatia and Phrygia.** Paul starts his third missionary journey in the Phrygian part of Galatia in central Asia Minor, near the Pisidian towns in which he and Barnabas planted churches on their first trip several years before.

verse_quote: Apollos ... eloquent ... competent in the Scriptures.
note: Apollos’s speaking ability and proficiency in the OT make him a strong encourager of fellow believers (v. 27) because he is a formidable gospel advocate in the Jewish community of Ephesus (v. 28).

verse_quote: fervent in spirit ... he knew only the baptism of John.
note: The description of Apollos’s ministry suggests that he is fervent in the (Holy) Spirit, unlike disciples of John the Baptist whom Paul will meet at Ephesus (19:1–7).

After finishing his ministry in Phrygian Galatia (18:23), Paul continues westward by land through the region of Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis (Col. 4:13) in the Lycus Valley, and finally arrives at Ephesus. Here he ministers for about three years (vv. 8, 10), from about A.D. 53 to 56.

**Ephesus.** The capital of the Roman province of Asia, Ephesus was founded in about the twelfth century B.C. by Ionians from Athens. It became a great commercial power, but its economic prosperity declined, mainly because erosion into the river had silted and clogged the harbor. The city derived wealth and prestige from its temple of Artemis, built in honor of the goddess of fertility. The Ephesus of Paul’s day has passed its zenith but is still an important commercial and religious center.

**some disciples.** According to v. 7, “about twelve.”

As followers of John the Baptist, these believers probably know that John foretold One who would baptize with the Spirit (Luke 3:16) but have not learned that John’s prophecy was fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit on the Day of Pentecost. As in John 7:39 (where the ESV rightly renders a Greek clause that literally reads, “the Spirit was not yet,” as “the Spirit had not been given”), probably these disciples’ response does not mean that they do not know of the Holy Spirit’s existence but that they do not know that He arrived in history and human experience at Pentecost, as promised through John and previous prophets such as Isaiah and Joel. Note that throughout Acts, all categories of people receive the baptism of the Holy Spirit: Jews, Samaritans, God-fearing Greeks, and other Gentiles.

verse_quote: baptism of repentance ... who was to come after him ... Jesus.
note: John’s baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3) was directed toward repentance of sins and looked forward to the redeeming work of Jesus.

The experience the Ephesian Gentiles have when receiving the Holy Spirit parallels that of the Jews (2:4, 11), Samaritans (8:14–17), and God-fearing Gentiles (10:44–46). This episode is an extension of the Pentecost experience to yet another group of people (v. 2 note), which indicates that Christ’s promise of the Spirit has now been extended to “the end of the earth,” as the third and last geographical territory to which the apostolic witness was to extend (as stated in Acts 1:8). “Prophesying” in this passage may be equivalent to “telling ... the mighty works of God” (2:11) or speaking so as to extol God (10:46).

Nothing further is known about Tyrannus. Some manuscripts add “from the fifth to the tenth hour” (11 A.M. to 4 P.M.). Tyrannus may use the room in the cool morning hours, giving it to Paul for the rest of the day.
The Roman province in the western part of Asia Minor. As a result of this teaching, groups of believers are formed in numerous places (Col. 4:13, 16; Rev. 2; 3).

That is, sweat cloths or work aprons that Paul uses as he works at making tents or awnings (18:3). As a touch of faith on the hem of Jesus’ garment brought healing to a woman (Luke 8:44, 48) and Peter’s shadow was apparently instrumental in healing others (Acts 5:15, 16), so now in a pagan city God attests the truth of His gospel and the authority of His messenger with “extraordinary miracles” (19:11).

**to the sick.** This is not Paul’s doing; because of their pagan religious background, the Ephesians are used to employing superstitious means (v. 19). God accommodates His gracious work to their ignorance.

In ancient times, it was common practice to use magical names to drive out evil spirits. Jews in Ephesus presume “to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus” over those possessed, trying to imitate what Paul does (v. 12; 16:18). As the site of the famous temple of Artemis (v. 24 note), Ephesus attracted religious (pagan) pilgrims from throughout the empire. Papyri containing lists of divine names to be invoked in exorcisms, traced to Ephesus, have been found across the Mediterranean world.

The evil spirit perceives that Sceva’s sons lack faith in Jesus and therefore have no authority to invoke His name. The saving power of Jesus’ name is conveyed not by reciting its syllables but by trusting the person who bears the name (3:16).

These are scrolls with the names and incantations used in their magic.

**fifty thousand pieces of silver.** Probably a reference to the Attic drachma. Divergent opinions concerning ancient-to-modern exchange rates and comparative standards of living make it difficult to estimate equivalent values in today’s currencies, but Luke obviously preserves this figure to illustrate the depth of the conversion experienced by many who had practiced the dark arts but who now, freed through Christ, gladly destroy their extremely valuable occult libraries.

This summary of the Word’s growth echoes and elaborates earlier summary statements (6:7; 12:24; 13:49).

**19:20 the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.** This summary of the growth of the word of the Lord echoes and elaborates earlier summary statements (6:7; 12:24; 13:49) to indicate the linear journey of the gospel (in Judea, then Samaria, and finally in the rest of the world, according to the outline of Acts 1:8). This coalesces with the repetition of the Pentecost experience earlier in the chapter (19:2–6), which also indicated that the witness of the Spirit was to travel to the three geographical areas of Jerusalem–Judea, Samaria, and the “end of the earth.” Recall that this is an allusion to Ex. 1:7, 12, 20, “multiplied and grew strong” (on which see 6:7 and which occurs also in 12:24). Hence, throughout Acts a new exodus is happening to new Israel through belief in Jesus, the Lord of the new exodus. Recall also that “the word of God” is an allusion to God’s Word prophesied to accomplish restoration in Isaiah (especially Is. 2:3, and its developments in Is. 45:22–24 and 55:10, 11). Here that prophecy of restoration is viewed as continuing to be fulfilled through belief in Jesus.

Presumably, Paul sends these helpers to Macedonia to motivate and organize the Gentile churches’ offering for needy believers in Jerusalem and Judea, as he sent Titus and another trusted brother to Corinth in Achaia for this purpose (2 Cor. 8:1–6, 16–24).
See note on 9:2.

An important guild of silversmiths developed at Ephesus on account of the large numbers of religious pilgrims. The pilgrims came to worship the goddess Diana (Artemis in Greek) who was portrayed by a famous statue at Ephesus as a fertility goddess. Her “image” that had fallen “from the sky” (v. 35) was probably a meteorite that the people had begun to worship. The temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Not only was it the destination of religious pilgrimage, but it was a banking depository as well. Making silver shrines and images of the goddess was a trade important to the city’s economic well-being.

verse_quote: temple of the great goddess Artemis.
note: The archaic Ionic temple of Artemis measured 220 feet (67 m) by 425 feet (136 m), with 127 marble columns each 62 feet (19 m) high. The lowest drums of the thirty-six western columns were carved with reliefs. The statue of the goddess was displayed in an inner room of the temple. Demetrius and other silversmiths are alarmed by Paul’s persuasive words against idolatry not only because it threatens “this trade of ours” but also because it challenges the reputation of the goddess, her world-famous temple, and the city of Ephesus.
The Greek word _ekklēsia_ is used here and in vv. 39 and 41 to denote a secular civic assembly of people, where legal decisions are made concerning the management of the city (5:11 note).

verse_quote: neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess.
note: According to the first-century Jewish historian Josephus, these were common charges of Gentiles against Jews and Jewish Christians. If “sacrilegious” is construed literally as “temple robbers,” the town clerk is correct to claim that Paul and his team cannot be charged with this crime. On the other hand, in view of Paul’s remarks about idols in Athens (17:24, 25, 29), he may well have said things about Artemis and her glorious temple that her devotees would consider blasphemous. Luke records the official’s placating words without endorsing their accuracy, showing that the gospel’s opponents, not its advocates, have been responsible for the civil disruptions, the violations of Roman law and order, that have accompanied the gospel’s dissemination (cf. 16:19–24, 36–39; 18:12–17).

Paul goes up the coast of Asia Minor from Ephesus, either by road or by ship, probably as far as Troas and then by ship to Macedonia (cf. 16:8–10) and Philippi (cf. 16:11–40), visiting groups of believers on the way. While in Macedonia, Paul may extend his ministry as far as Illyricum (modern Albania; Rom. 15:19). His decision to visit the churches of Macedonia first, before moving south to those in Achaia, is a change of intentions that he previously communicated to the church at Corinth. Some in Corinth will accuse him of vacillation, a charge that he answers forthrightly in terms of his pastoral sensitivity to the Corinthians’ spiritual need (2 Cor. 1:15–24; 2:12, 13; 7:5–9).

Paul arrives at Corinth, where he spends the winter of A.D. 56–57. During this time he writes his epistle to the Romans, announcing his plan to deliver an offering from Gentile churches to believers in Judea before setting off for Rome, a journey which he has long desired to make (Rom. 1:11–15; 15:23, 24, 26).

Paul’s traveling companions are listed by name. They may be official church representatives appointed to travel with Paul to deliver money collected for relief of the Jerusalem church (1 Cor. 16:1–4; 2 Cor. 9:1–5). Sopater may be the “Sosipater” mentioned in Rom. 16:21. Aristarchus faithfully accompanied Paul during the third missionary journey (19:29), and he later accompanies the apostle to Rome (27:2) where he shares Paul’s imprisonment (Col. 4:10). Secundus is not mentioned elsewhere in the NT. Gaius is from Derbe in Lycaonia (central Asia Minor), a different man from the Macedonian Gaius mentioned in 19:29. On Timothy, see 16:1–3 and Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion. Tychicus is later Paul’s representative to various churches during the apostle’s imprisonments (Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7–9; 2 Tim. 4:12). Trophimus accompanies Paul to Jerusalem, where his presence in the city (though not in a forbidden section of the temple, as opponents allege) leads to Paul’s arrest (21:29). He apparently later accompanies Paul after the apostle’s release from his first Roman imprisonment (2 Tim. 4:20).
Luke again uses the first person plural pronoun, indicating that he traveled with Paul to Jerusalem.

Sunday, which was sanctified by Jesus’ resurrection and first appearances to His followers (John 20:19, 26) and apparently became the regular day for the churches’ assemblies for worship (1 Cor. 16:2).

**to break bread.** Since they are gathered together for worship on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day (Rev. 1:10), this celebration includes communion (2:42)—which on this occasion is observed well after midnight (20:11)—and is not just a fellowship meal (2:46).

**Paul talked.** This is a Sunday evening preaching-teaching service that also includes, as a central element, the breaking of bread in remembrance of Jesus’ sacrificial death.

Luke records that Eutychus was “taken up dead,” the likely result of such a fall. Paul’s restoration of the young man to life is one of two such raisings of the dead by apostles recorded in Acts (9:40; cf. Luke 7:11–17; 8:49–56; John 11:1–44).
Paul goes by road the twenty miles (32 km) from Troas to Assos, while Luke travels with the ship.

verse_quote: the following day ... Chios ... Samos ... Miletus.
note: They sail down the coast to Miletus, about thirty miles (48 km) south of Ephesus.
These are the ordained representatives of the Ephesian congregation, called to be overseers and shepherds of the church of God (v. 28; cf. 1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9).

verse_quote: teaching you in public and from house to house.
note: Paul’s teaching during his three-year stay (v. 31) in Ephesus was extensive, including public lectures at the synagogue and the lecture hall of Tyrannus (19:8–10), as well as more private instruction in homes.
See note on 3:19. Both Jews and Gentiles must come to God in the same way—in repentance for sin (26:20; cf. Luke 24:47) and faith in Jesus Christ.

This probably refers to the direction of the Holy Spirit (19:21). Such explicit guidance by the Holy Spirit has often occurred during Paul’s ministry (16:6–10). The Spirit also reveals that suffering awaits Paul in Jerusalem (v. 23), a prediction that other Christians understand as a reason for Paul to avoid Jerusalem (21:11, 12), despite the Holy Spirit’s insistence that he must go there.

Paul’s statement is based on his own judgment of the situation rather than on divine revelation. Because of continued plots against his life by the Jews (v. 3), the divine revelation that “imprisonment and afflictions” await him (v. 23), and his own intention to focus his future ministry on the western Mediterranean (Rom. 15:23–29), Paul considers it likely that he is seeing the Ephesian elders for the last time. However, it appears that Paul is later able to return to Ephesus after his release from prison in Rome (1 Tim. 1:3).

verse_quote: innocent of the blood of all.
note: As a watchman on a city wall must sound the alarm of impending attack, so God’s spokesmen are responsible to warn their hearers of divine judgment to come on those who do not repent. Paul has delivered the message entrusted to him, so he bears no blame for those who refuse it (Ezek. 3:16–21; 33:1–9).

The revelation of God culminating in His Son, Jesus Christ. Paul, in his ministry to the Ephesians, did not suppress any truths of the gospel, “anything that was profitable” to his hearers (v. 20), but preached the full gospel to Jew and Gentile. Throughout his ministry, he always uses tact and discretion but never compromises the good news.

Many ancient manuscripts have a different word order, reading “the blood of His own,” that is, of Christ. On either reading, the elders’ duty to protect God’s church is shown by the infinite price He paid to purchase it for Himself (John 10:11, 14, 15).

The phrasing is remarkable in the way it acknowledges that the blood of Christ is the blood of God. This points to the hypostatic union, the union of a complete human nature and the complete divine nature in the one person of Christ. Because of this union, the attributes of one nature—in this case blood, an attribute of His human nature—can be attributed to the one person of Christ, who as the second person of the Trinity, is very God of very God. The divine nature and human nature are united in the one person of Christ “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of natures being in no way annulled by the union, but rather the characteristics of each nature being preserved” (Definition of the Council of Chalcedon). In other words, the human nature does not take on uniquely divine attributes such as omnipresence and omniscience, and the divine nature does not take on uniquely creaturely attributes such as the possibility of change and various limitations in knowledge and power. Because the two natures are united in the one person of Christ, we may distinguish but not separate them. For example, when the Bible speaks of Christ sleeping (Mark 4:38), that is a manifestation of His humanity. The person of Christ in that case experienced tiredness according to His human nature, not His divine nature, for the divine nature has no need of sleep (Ps. 121:3, 4).

Paul’s prophetic warning in this verse was fulfilled as the Ephesian church was soon to be plagued by false teachers, some of whom apparently were leaders of the church (1 Tim. 1:3, 7, 19, 20; 6:3–5; Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues).

Like Israel’s prophet-judge Samuel (1 Sam. 12:3–5), Paul does not serve God’s people for the sake of material gain, nor should the elders who will shepherd the church in the future (1 Pet. 5:2; 1 Tim. 3:3).

verse_quote: the words of the Lord Jesus.
note: The saying cited by Paul is not preserved in any of the Gospels, but must have been circulated orally by the apostles. For Jesus’ expressions of the thought, see Matt. 10:8; Luke 6:30, 31; 14:12–14.
The ancient Christian practice of the kiss of greeting (Luke 7:45; 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14) is still practiced by Christians in some cultures today.

They sail on a direct course through the islands off the coast of Asia Minor to the port of Patara. The small island of Cos was a free state in the province of Asia. Rhodes, the capital on the north end of the island of Rhodes, was famous and prosperous in the earlier Greek period. Patara, a port on the southwest coast of Asia Minor, was an important harbor for ancient ships sailing the eastern Mediterranean, thus bringing Syria, Palestine, and Egypt into contact with Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Achaia.
Syria controlled Phoenicia in the Roman period.
This port, famous in OT times and conquered by Alexander the Great, was about four hundred miles (644 km) southeast of Patara, a sea journey of about five days.

Paul is not disobedient to the Spirit; the Holy Spirit is compelling him to go to Jerusalem (20:22 note), while also giving prophecies that hardship awaits him there (20:23). In response to such predictions, Paul’s friends, assuming that he should avoid such suffering if possible, tried to persuade Paul “not to go on to Jerusalem” (cf. vv. 11, 12).

verse_quote: they all, with wives and children.
note: En route to Jerusalem (20:16), Paul’s team enjoys a week of fellowship with “the disciples” in Tyre, a sizable congregation of believing families that was planted through the testimony of scattered Christians after Stephen’s martyrdom (11:19).
A port twenty-five miles (40 km) south of Tyre, where the ship unloads its cargo.

This seaport, built by Herod the Great, was the provincial capital of Judea and located thirty-two miles (51 km) south of Ptolemais (10:1 note). Cornelius and the troops he commanded had been stationed there (10:1), and Paul is later held there for several years in Roman custody (23:23–26:32).

**Philip the evangelist ... one of the seven.** One of the seven chosen to handle the food distribution (6:1–6). He has preached to the Samaritans, the Ethiopian eunuch, and the people along the Palestinian coast (ch. 8). Although originally ordained to perform mercy ministry within the church, his gospel witness to Samaria, the Ethiopian, and the coastal towns warrants the title _evangelist_, an office mentioned rarely in the NT (Eph. 4:11; 2 Tim. 4:5).
The same Agabus who fifteen years earlier prophesied the severe famine in Judea and the surrounding area (11:27, 28).

In the first-century context of the apostles, Agabus, as a prophet, is led directly by the Spirit to give God’s inspired message.

**the Jews in Jerusalem will bind.** As events unfold, Roman troops will take Paul into protective custody to prevent his being harmed by a mob of Jews (22:22–29). Yet the result is Paul’s captivity by the Romans, initiated by his Jewish countrymen and prolonged by their leaders (24:1–9), as Paul himself sums up the situation in 28:17. Paul is thus to follow the same pattern of suffering that happened with Jesus. Agabus’s prophetic act with Paul’s belt and his abbreviated explanation accurately forecast events that will transpire when Paul reaches Jerusalem.

verse_quote: for the name of the Lord Jesus.
note: Like those who were apostles before his call, Paul considers it an honor to suffer disgrace for Jesus’ name (5:41).

Pentecost, the fiftieth day after Passover, is fast approaching (they have spent at least thirty-six days traveling from Philippi to Caesarea, and they have spent several days at Caesarea), and Paul wants to be at Jerusalem for this feast (20:16).

Jesus’ half-brother (Gal. 1:19) articulated the conclusion of the council of apostles and elders that secured Gentile believers’ freedom from the imposition of the entire law of Moses. He was also respected even by the Jewish community outside the church for his prayer life and his scrupulous observance of the law’s stipulations.

Thousands of Jewish Christians in Jerusalem strictly observe the Mosaic law. While many of these no doubt resent the fact that Gentile Christians are not required to observe the ceremonial law of Moses (v. 25; 15:1–31), the charge here is that Paul has been encouraging Jews to forsake the law as well (v. 21).
