Such a charge may have been prompted by reports that Paul himself does not follow the Jewish ceremonial law when in Gentile company. Though Paul has no objection to Jews’ following their ancestral customs and does so when ministering to Jews (16:3; 18:18; see 1 Cor. 9:20), he opposes any attempt to impose the observance of Mosaic ceremonial laws on Gentiles, or to make such observance in some way necessary for salvation (Rom. 14:1–8; Gal. 2:3; 5:2–6). Always careful to avoid giving unnecessary offense, Paul’s flexibility in such matters shows that the interests of the gospel are always foremost in his mind (1 Cor. 9:19–23). He even counsels Jewish believers in Corinth against a misguided attempt to reverse their circumcision (1 Cor. 7:18, 19).

This is the Nazirite vow (Num. 6:1–21), during which the devotee let his hair grow. When the period of the vow was over, he shaved off his hair, dedicated it to the Lord, and burned it together with the sacrifice for the fellowship offering (Num. 6:18). Paul pays the expenses for four Nazirites, goes to the priest with them for the sacrifices, and participates in the purification rites. In this way, Paul publicly demonstrates the falsehood of the rumor circulating about him in Jerusalem (18:18 note).

verse_quote: brought Greeks into the temple ... defiled this holy place.
note: Placards on the low wall separating the courtyard of the Gentiles from that of the (Israelite) women sharply warned uncircumcised males not to proceed beyond that point to enter the areas nearer to the temple building itself. Paul’s accusers, Jews from Asia, assume and allege without proof that he has brought an Ephesian Gentile colleague into a forbidden area of the temple precincts.
The tribune is surprised to hear Paul speak Greek; he has thought him to be an insurrectionist Jew from Egypt who three years before had appeared there claiming to be a prophet.
Lit. “dagger men,” militant Jewish nationalists.

Probably the stairs leading from the temple area to the Antonia Fortress (rebuilt by Herod the Great and named after Mark Antony) on the north edge of the temple platform.

**Hebrew language.** Perhaps Aramaic, as commonly spoken by Jews in Palestine, although the priests and Levites would also have known Hebrew, and some archaeological evidence suggests that Hebrew was still in everyday use by some Palestinian Jews. In the setting of the temple and in answer to accusations of disloyalty toward Judaism, a well-trained Pharisee may well have addressed the crowd in Hebrew (22:2). Greek was the common language of the Roman and Mediterranean world.

An important city, located in Cilicia on the eastern Mediterranean coast north of Cyprus. It was a noted intellectual center.

**22:3 educated at the feet of Gamaliel.** Gamaliel was a respected scholar (5:33–39) and leader of the school of Hillel, one of the two influential rabbinical movements in first-century Judaism.

This frequent identification of the Christian movement (19:9, 23; 24:14, 22; see 18:26) may have been derived from Jesus’ self-description (John 14:6) or from an OT metaphor (Gen. 18:19; Deut. 8:6; Ps. 18:21). However, most likely it was a name that had its source in Is. 40:3 (“In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD”), part of a restoration and second exodus prophecy about Israel’s deliverance, so that the very name of the Christian movement was understood to express the idea that Christians were the fulfillment of the prophecies of Israel’s restoration (see the Introduction: Acts in the Larger Story of the Bible).

An appropriate person to meet Saul, who was a zealous Pharisee, “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Phil. 3:5, 6). Being known to Ananias would recommend Paul to other Jews in the city who would otherwise be suspicious of him (9:10–19).
Saul heard Stephen apply this title of the Suffering Servant to Jesus (7:52; Is. 53:11) in the moments before Stephen’s martyrdom.

Baptism in the NT is an outward sign of an inward cleansing. As such, it parallels circumcision in the OT (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Ezek. 44:7).

Echoing Is. 57:19 (Eph. 2:17), Paul’s vision in the very temple that he is now charged with defiling revealed that his own people would reject his message but the Gentiles would welcome it, as Paul has seen in his travels (13:45–49).

The Roman scourge was a whip of leather thongs loaded with bits of metal or bone; it could maim for life or kill. Jesus was scourged with such a whip (John 19:1). Thus far, Paul has been beaten (Acts 16:22, 23; 2 Cor. 11:24, 25) but has never endured this severe punishment, which would not be inflicted on a Roman citizen without legal due process.
The soldiers either stretch Paul’s arms around a pole to expose his back or tie his hands and hoist him from the ground to administer the whipping.

Paul appeals again to his Roman citizenship, knowing that he is going to be punished without trial (16:37). Roman citizenship was highly prized, usually given only to those of high position or those who had performed some valuable service to the state. It was then passed on to one’s family, as in Paul’s case, since he is “a citizen by birth” (v. 28).
Son of Nebedaeus, a brutal and violent man who ruled as high priest from A.D. 48–59. This is not the earlier Annas of John 18:13. Ananias was assassinated early in the war with Rome (A.D. 66–70).

Tombs were often whitewashed to make them more visible (Matt. 23:27, 28), so Paul’s metaphor may mean that Ananias’s splendid outward appearance only conceals the decay of death within. He may also be alluding to the imagery of Ezek. 13:8–16, in which whitewash on a wall enhances its appearance but does not add to its strength. Paul aptly characterizes a corrupt ruler whose abuse of authority demeans his priestly office.

**contrary to the law.** According to Jewish law, Paul must be tried and found guilty before being punished.

verse_quote: I did not know ... for it is written.
note: Paul’s response to the bystanders’ rebuke implies that, however deserving Ananias is of divine retribution, respect for the high priest’s office would have restrained the apostle’s retort, had he recognized that the council member who ordered that Paul be assaulted was, in fact, the high priest. God’s law (Ex. 22:28) obligates Paul to respect the people’s leader even when a ruler is not behaving respectably, just as David honored Saul, the Lord’s anointed, although the king sought to kill David (1 Sam. 24:3–15).

These two groups emerged during the historical period between the events described in the OT and the events recorded in the NT. They had different political and religious views. Paul seizes the opportunity to emphasize their religious differences by identifying himself as a Pharisee and a believer in the resurrection of the dead, against the Sadducees, who denied a future bodily resurrection and the existence of angels and spirits (v. 8; cf. 4:1, 2; Matt. 22:23–32).
These are teachers, expert interpreters of Jewish law. Paul’s appeal to a tenet that sets their party apart from the Sadducees inclines them to come to his defense.

verse_quote: you must testify also in Rome.
note: This encouragement given by special revelation from the Lord assures Paul of his survival to bring the gospel to the imperial capital, as Christ granted him a similarly encouraging vision in Corinth (18:9, 10). A host of obstacles—assassination conspiracies, legal delays, storm, shipwreck, and snakebite—will arise to threaten this promise, but none can prevent its fulfillment (27:23–26)

Evidently some members of Paul’s family are in Jerusalem.

**told Paul.** Prisoners received their necessary supplies from relatives and friends who regularly visited them.
Heavily equipped infantry and cavalry delivers Paul safely to Felix, the procurator of the imperial province of Judea. The official provincial headquarters is at Caesarea., 24

Felix was addressed as “most excellent Felix” (24:2) during his eight-year administration. The Roman historian Tacitus said that Felix “occupied the office of a king while having the mind of a slave, saturated with cruelty and lust.”

verse_quote: having learned that he was a Roman citizen.
note: The tribune prudently omits the detail that he had ordered Paul’s flogging before he learned of his Roman citizenship.

A town built by Herod the Great in honor of his father, Antipater, about thirty miles (48 km) northwest of Jerusalem. The distance covered overnight puts the party beyond the reach of the would-be assassins, so the two hundred spearmen on foot return to Jerusalem while the seventy mounted on horses press on more quickly, conducting Paul to the governor’s palace in the provincial capital, Caesarea Maritima.
The official residence built by Herod the Great. It became a Roman praetorium or official residence and included prisoners’ cells (John 18:28; Phil. 1:13).
As an orator, Tertullus is a kind of lawyer, possibly a Jew (he refers to Jewish law as “our” law; v. 6 text note).

verse_quote: through you we enjoy much peace.
note: Tertullus’s flattery to curry the governor’s favor is contradicted by records that show that Felix’s tenure as governor was marred by brutal repression and violent acts against the populace of the province, both Jews and Samaritans.

Tertullus charges that Paul is a chronic troublemaker, the leader of a disreputable religious sect, and a person who has threatened to profane the temple (see 21:27–29). Paul replies to these accusations in his defense before Felix (vv. 10–21).

**24:5 the Nazarenes.** Christians at this time were identified as followers of Jesus of Nazareth. “Nazareth” may have been a term of contempt (John 1:46).

Paul assures Felix that as a Jew he follows a religion protected by Rome. As a follower of “the Way,” Paul worships the “God of our fathers”; believes the faith revealed in Israel’s Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets; and even shares his accusers’ hope in the resurrection of the dead (Ps. 16:9, 10; Dan. 12:1, 2; Acts 13:34–37; 1 Thess. 4:13–18; 2 Thess. 1:8).

Conveniently absent are those who incited the mob in the temple by alleging (without ground) that Paul had brought an uncircumcised Ephesian believer into a forbidden courtyard of the temple (21:27–29). So, there are no witnesses present to testify to the original occasion that brought Paul into Roman custody., 19

Before the Sanhedrin, Paul’s only controversial statement has nothing to do with Roman political interests, but concerns an issue internal to Judaism, a longstanding doctrinal disagreement between two established parties, the Sadducees and the Pharisees (23:6–10).

verse_quote: a rather accurate knowledge of the Way.
note: Felix knows enough to realize that the charges against Paul and the Christian movement are baseless, and even sends for Paul subsequently and repeatedly to learn more about faith in Jesus the Messiah (vv. 24, 26). His guilty conscience is struck with fear when Paul speaks of the coming judgment (v. 25); but he lacks the integrity to resist the hope of a bribe from Paul (v. 26) and the pressure of the Jewish leadership (v. 27).
As a Roman citizen whose case is still pending, Paul is given some freedom (28:16).

Daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1–23) and sister of Herod Agrippa II (25:13; 26:3 note) and Bernice (25:13 note). Drusilla left Azizus, king of Emesa in Syria, to marry Felix. She probably died along with her son Agrippa in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius at Pompeii, A.D. 79.
Festus is from a noble family in Rome. Though Felix was greedy and evil, Festus is wise and honorable.

Since Felix has kept Paul in custody in Caesarea for two years (24:27), presumably the assassins who earlier vowed to fast until they killed Paul (23:14) have violated their vow. Yet the plot to ambush and slay the apostle still simmers among the leadership of the Sanhedrin.

Festus must protect Paul while he was in Roman custody. Probably having reviewed the letter from the tribune Claudius Lysias (23:26–30) that explains Paul’s relocation to custody in the provincial capital, Caesarea, Festus refuses the request of the Jews, saving Paul from their plot.

verse_quote: wishing to do the Jews a favor.
note: Although generally more just and judicious than his predecessors, Festus’s political pragmatism replicates the craven expedience of Felix (24:27) and Pontius Pilate (Luke 23:4, 5, 13–24).

Fearing that Festus is going to grant the Jews their request, Paul exercises his right as a Roman citizen to be tried before Caesar (Nero) in Rome. At this time, Nero has not yet shown his hostility to Christianity. Paul could hope to be acquitted by Nero, particularly since his opponents have presented to the provincial governors no evidence whatsoever that he has violated imperial law (25:18, 19, 25–27; see 26:31, 32).

This is Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I (who martyred James the son of Zebedee and would have done the same to Peter if he could have; 12:1–19) and great-grandson of Herod the Great (26:3 note). Agrippa II was favored by Nero with an expansion of his domain in northern Palestine, so his expert opinion on Paul’s case will carry weight with the Emperor.

**Bernice.** The oldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, Bernice was twice widowed before entering into what was alleged to be an incestuous relationship with her brother, Herod Agrippa II. Despite the scandal of this relationship, she was frequently presented as Herod’s queen on official occasions (e.g., vv. 13, 23).

verse_quote: certain points of dispute ... about their own religion.
note: Like Gallio in Corinth, Festus concludes that the controversy between Paul and his opponents concerns matters internal to Judaism and involve no violation of Roman law (18:12–17). Unlike Gallio, who could dismiss the Jewish minority in Achaia without political fallout, Festus does not risk angering the community leaders in Judaea by daring to release Paul from custody.

verse_quote: I have nothing definite to write.
note: To refer a Roman citizen’s case to the emperor, rather than resolving it locally, entails some political jeopardy for a provincial governor, particularly if he cannot articulate alleged crimes against the empire that warrant further legal process rather than the prisoner’s exoneration and release.

verse_quote: familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews.
note: As the great-grandson of Herod the Great and son of Herod Agrippa I, who had persecuted the church (12:1–23), Herod Agrippa II (A.D. 27–c. 100) has an intimate knowledge of Jewish matters. Although influential in Jewish religious affairs because he had political authority to appoint the high priest, Agrippa II was unpopular with the Jews because of his incestuous relationship with his sister Bernice (25:13 note).

verse_quote: strictest party ... I have lived as a Pharisee.
note: Knowing the background of Agrippa, Paul stresses his dependence on the God of his fathers (cf. 24:14) and his link to the Pharisees (Phil. 3:5, 6) in order to show that he continues to identify himself as a Jew.
Paul argues that God has promised the resurrection of the body. Although this is the belief of Jews in general and the Pharisees in particular, it is being used as the basis of charges against him.

Paul’s experience on the road to Damascus (9:1–19) is so important to him that he recounts it twice, once before the Jewish crowd in the temple courtyard (22:6–16), and again before a Roman governor and a minor monarch whose family has ruled the Jewish people on Rome’s behalf for several generations.

verse_quote: delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles.
note: The record of Acts has borne witness to Christ’s rescue of Paul from death at the hands of his Jewish kinsmen (9:29, 30; 13:50; 17:5–9; 18:12–17; 21:27–36; 23:12–35; 25:1–12) and of the Gentiles (14:19, 20; 16:19–39; 19:23–41), to whom he was commissioned (22:21; cf. Rom. 11:13).
See 2:38; 3:19 and note; 17:30, 31; 20:21; theological note “Repentance.”

verse_quote: Christ must suffer ... rise from the dead.
note: First-century Jews had difficulty accepting the idea that the Messiah would suffer and die, as did Jesus’ disciples during His earthly ministry (Matt. 16:21–23; 17:22, 23). Jesus and His apostles taught this doctrine from the Scriptures (17:2, 3; Luke 24:27; 1 Cor. 15:3, 4), yet unbelieving Jews rejected it, arrested Paul, and sought to kill him.

Agrippa faces a dilemma: if he says no, he will anger the Jews; if he says yes, he will lose face because Paul will urge him to acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah, in response to the testimony of the prophetic Scriptures.

verse_quote: would you persuade me to be a Christian.
note: The king uses a delaying tactic, arguing that a brief speech is insufficient time to become a Christian. In the first century, “Christian” (cf. 11:26) was probably a term of contempt (1 Pet. 4:16).

verse_quote: nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.
note: The consensus reached by Festus and Agrippa is that Paul is not guilty of any grave violation of Roman law, a conclusion reached earlier by other imperial officials (16:39; 18:14, 15; 25:18–20, 25). Agrippa, who understands Jewish issues well (26:3), concludes that Paul could be released if he had not invoked his right as a Roman citizen to appeal his case to the emperor. Festus still has no statement of charges to send with the prisoner to the imperial court.
Six hundred Syrian soldiers under the governor’s direct command.

On the coast between Troas and Pergamum.

**we put to sea.** This chapter is filled with nautical terms and directions, confirming that the author was an eyewitness, as his use of the first-person-plural pronoun to refer to Paul’s party implies.

**we ... Aristarchus.** Paul has at least two companions with him: Luke as his physician (Col. 4:14) and Aristarchus (19:29; 20:4; Col. 4:10; Philem. 24) from Thessalonica, probably his attendant. His prison epistles mention others who were with him in Rome at some point, as he awaited the emperor’s decision on his appeal (Phil. 2:19; 30; Col. 4:7–14; Philem. 23, 24).

An eastern Mediterranean port, today in Lebanon. Paul and Barnabas encouraged Christians in this region as they traveled to the council of apostles and elders at Jerusalem (15:3), so it is natural that Paul has friends in this city.

**Julius treated Paul kindly.** The centurion’s respect for his prisoner will lead to the sparing of many lives in the storm at sea to come (vv. 31, 32, 42, 43).
That is, close under the eastern point of the island in order to be protected from the westerly winds of the summer and fall.
The ship goes up the Syrian coast, past Antioch of Syria and then west to Myra. In Paul’s day, Myra is an important port of call for grain ships sailing between Alexandria and Rome.
A port town with a small harbor on the southern coast of Crete, exposed to fierce winds from the Mediterranean during the stormy winter months.

The Day of Atonement, Israel’s only annual observance that required fasting, occurred in the autumn (late September to mid-October), when weather on the Mediterranean became unpredictable and sea travel precarious.

Paul’s advice is based on experience at sea (2 Cor. 11:25, 26), not divine revelation. The complete disaster that he anticipates will not be completely fulfilled, for by God’s grace there will be no loss of life (vv. 24–26, 44).

The captain and the owner want to reach the larger and safer harbor of Phoenix about forty miles (64 km) to the west, but in going west past Cape Matala, the ship will be exposed to winds from the northwest., 12
Now called Gozzo, this island lies about twenty miles (32 km) southwest of Crete’s western coast.

Because of the danger of violent storms on the Mediterranean, ancient vessels carried ropes that would be tied around the hull sideways in order to strengthen it in an emergency.

**lowered the gear.** Fearing that they might be driven all the way to the Syrtis (a region of sands near modern-day Libya and Tunisia), the sailors lower the sail. The description in Greek could also mean that they lowered a sea anchor to slow the ship down.

verse_quote: the God to whom I belong.
note: Christians are God’s property both by creation (Ps. 100:3) and by redemption (1 Cor. 6:19, 20).

As in earlier crises, the Lord speaks special reassurance to quiet Paul’s fears (18:9, 10; 23:11).

**granted you all ... with you.** In His kindness, God will save everyone on the ship from drowning.
The island of Malta (28:1), south of Sicily.

God’s assurance that no lives will be lost (vv. 24, 34) is certain, yet the means necessary to that end are that the sailors and their nautical expertise remain on the ship until it ran aground.

Terror and seasickness extinguished appetites as the storm raged for two weeks (v. 21), but Paul knows that food will supply strength to swim, another means to the fulfillment of God’s promise to save everyone on board.

verse_quote: not a hair is to perish from ... any.
note: God is in control of the minute details of life (Luke 21:18). God’s sure promise (vv. 22–24) has corrected Paul’s earlier expectation that there would be loss of life (v. 10).
This number of passengers on an ancient seagoing vessel is not unusual. Some ships of the period could carry considerably more.

See text note. This is the narrow channel in St. Paul’s Bay between Malta and the island of Salmonetta, where the currents create sandbars. This sort of nautical detail indicates that Luke was an eyewitness of the event.
Soldiers who allowed prisoners to escape could expect humiliation at best and execution at worst (12:19; 16:27).
The centurion Julius’s admiration for Paul (v. 3) lies behind his order that his troops spare all prisoners—another means to the fulfillment of God’s promise (27:24).

Ancient Melita (the name means “a place of refuge”) was settled by Phoenicians who came there about 1000 B.C. Malta measures eight miles (13 km) by eighteen miles (29 km) and is sixty miles (97 km) south of Sicily and 180 miles (290 km) northeast of Cyrene, North Africa.

The Greek word is “barbarians” (Rom. 1:14; Col. 3:11), a term of disparagement used by urbane Greeks to demean “rustics” who clung to their own languages (in Malta, Phoenician) rather than becoming fluent in Greek, the empire’s _lingua franca._

Being cold-blooded, snakes can become stiff and motionless in cold weather, and Paul must have picked up the serpent along with the brush. Some have suggested that the snake is nonpoisonous, but the Greek word translated “creature” in v. 4 is one applied to dangerous animals and poisonous snakes, and there is little reason to doubt the islanders’ identification of the snake as poisonous.
The Maltese concluded that, although the Roman prisoner Paul has escaped the shipwreck, the goddess Dike (justice) is using the venomous viper to inflict the punishment that a criminal deserves.

There is irony in the islanders’ reappraisal of Paul’s character—from murderer destined for death to that of a god. This recalls the events in Lystra, where first the people hailed Paul and Barnabas as gods, and then nearly stoned Paul to death (14:11–20).

Octavius Augustus installed a Roman governor on Malta. In inscriptions, his office is “the chief man over all the municipality of Malta.” This fits Luke’s description of Publius as “the chief man of the island.” Publius shows the visitors hospitality at his island estate.
The Greek words suggest repeated feverish attacks. The ailment has been diagnosed in modern times as Malta fever, caused by the milk of Maltese goats.

verse_quote: honored us greatly ... put on board whatever we needed.
note: Though despised by Greeks and Romans as barbarians, the residents of Malta are distinguished by their hospitality and generosity.

No doubt it carries Egyptian wheat to Rome, the imperial capital.

**the twin gods.** Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus in Greek mythology, were considered the patron deities of seafarers.
On the eastern coast of the island of Sicily, just south of Italy.
As at Sidon when their voyage began (27:3), the centurion again honors Paul by allowing him to enjoy the fellowship of Italian Christians for an entire week before conducting him to Rome.

verse_quote: Paul thanked God and took courage.
note: When he wrote to the believers in Rome several years earlier, he anticipated his and their mutual encouragement through each other’s faith (Rom. 1:11, 12). That anticipation is now fulfilled.

Under house arrest, Paul lives in his own rented home (v. 30). There he can entertain his friends and minister to groups such as the Roman Jews. He also seizes opportunities to speak of Christ to his guards (Phil. 1:13).
When he invoked his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor, Paul had no desire to direct Caesar’s unfavorable attention to the Jewish people.

verse_quote: no letters ... none ... has reported ... any evil against you.
note: Apparently the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, realizing that its accusations against Paul will not stand up in Roman law (25:25; 26:31, 32), have not sent a delegation to the imperial court, nor even communicated with the Jewish community in Rome.

Paul’s ministry in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia concluded with a citation from Isaiah (13:47, citing Is. 49:6) and an announcement that the gospel that had been rejected by unbelieving Jews would be proclaimed to the Gentiles. Likewise, Acts concludes the account of Paul’s ministry in Rome with a quotation from Isaiah concerning Israel’s dull hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes (Is. 6:9, 10), and the declaration that God is sending his salvation to Gentiles, who will heed His word. These Jews continue to fulfill the prophecy of Israel’s hardening that began even in Isaiah’s own time and continued up until the time of Christ (e.g., see Matt. 13:14’s “fulfilled” that introduces the same Is. 6:9, 10 text) and even up until Paul’s own day.

From A.D. 60 to 62, Paul was under house arrest preaching and teaching to anyone who wanted to hear. His subject is summarized as the kingdom of God and Jesus Christ. At the end of Acts, Paul has not yet been tried before Nero, as the Lord said was going to happen (27:24). It appears that Paul expected to be acquitted and released (Phil. 1:25; 2:24; Philem. 22). This must have occurred before A.D. 64, when Nero set fire to Rome and accused Christians of that crime. When released, Paul seems to have taken up his ministry again, going as far as Greece (Nicopolis, Titus 3:12; Thessalonica, 2 Tim. 4:10), Crete (Titus 1:5), and Asia Minor (Ephesus, 2 Tim. 1:18; 4:12; Troas, 2 Tim. 4:13; Miletus, 2 Tim. 4:20). Possibly he went as far west as Spain (Rom. 15:23, 24, 28), as the first-century writing 1 Clement may indicate. In about A.D. 67, Paul was imprisoned again by Nero and executed. In 2 Tim. 4:6–8, Paul anticipates the end of his life.

**28:31 with all boldness and without hindrance.** For Paul, Luke, and those who followed, the message about Jesus and the glorious kingdom of God was to go on in triumph. From his second Roman imprisonment (see previous note) Paul observed that, though he himself was in chains, “the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). The last Greek word of Acts (rendered “without hindrance” in the ESV) makes the same point.
